Upon direct examination by the Taxpayer’s Representatives, the Tax
Auditor testified that: (1) Taxpayer Exhibit 2 contains Notices of Proposed
Assessments and Explanations of Tax Adjustments for the years in the audit
periods; (2) the Explanation of Tax Adjustment for 2013 states that, “Per
Arkansas Tax Code 1.26-51-504(a) your other state tax credit has been
disallowed. You can not take a deduction for gambling losses and a tax credit for
taxes paid to other states on the winnings”;9 (3) Department Exhibit 36 is a copy
of Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation 1.26-51-504(a); (4) the Regulation
does not prohibit taking a deduction for gambling losses (there is no reference to
gambling at all) and a credit for taxes paid to another state on the winnings; (5) a
credit and a deduction can be taken at the same time (contrary to the second
sentence on the Explanation of Tax Adjustment); (6) the Taxpayer owed income
taxes to for the years in the audit period; (7) the example in the
Regulation would be different if the income of Mrs. Jones was gambling winnings
from and there was a full deduction for the amount of income (the
credit in the example would be $0.00);10 (8) the Taxpayer was charged no tax in
Arkansas on the gambling winnings from because there was a
deduction for gambling losses equal to the amount of gambling winnings; (9) the
Taxpayer’s income tax liability to the State of was based on the method
of calculation used by the State of ; (10) to make the adjustments in
this matter, he relied on Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 (Supp. 2017) and Arkansas
Individual Income Tax Regulation 1.26-51-504(a) (this statute and regulation are

Upon cross-examination by the Department’s Representative, the Tax
Auditor testified that: (1) the first sentence of the second paragraph of Arkansas
Individual Income Tax Regulation 1.26-51-504(a) is a limitation on the ability of
a taxpayer to take the credit (a taxpayer can’t get a refund from Arkansas for
taxes paid to other states); (2) the effect of the second sentence of the second
12

paragraph of Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation 1.26-51-504(a) is that a
taxpayer has to prove double taxation on a portion of income (the Taxpayer’s
gambling winnings from were possibly subject to double taxation (for
2013, $ )); (3) did not tax any portion of the Taxpayer’s
Arkansas source income, was only taxing source income;
and (4) the Taxpayer owed more total income taxes (Arkansas and ) by
virtue of gambling in but that result is not a function of Arkansas law.
Upon re-direct examination by the Taxpayer’s Representatives, the Tax
Auditor testified that: (1) with respect to the second sentence of the second
paragraph of Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation 1.26-51-504(a), the
Taxpayer has to clearly show that he has been double taxed on any portion of his
income in order to get the credit;11 and (2) was only allowed to tax the
Taxpayer’s gambling winnings (there was no jurisdiction for to tax his
Arkansas income).
Upon direct examination by the Department’s Representative, the Tax
Auditor testified that: (1) his statement on the 2013 Explanation of Tax

Upon cross-examination by the Taxpayer’s Representatives, the Tax
Auditor testified that: (1) the taxes paid by the Taxpayer to were
allowed as an itemized deduction but not as a credit; (2) an Arkansas income tax
return does not ask for the amount of tax paid on just source income;
(3) the Instructions for the AR1000TC (See Department Exhibit 37) state that,
“This credit cannot exceed the Arkansas income tax on the same income . . .” but
the instructions do not include the words “source income”; (4) source income is
needed in order to determine if there is double taxation; (5) Arkansas Individual
Income Tax Regulation 1.26-51-504(a) does not make a distinction between
income or source income; (6) Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation 1.26-
51-504(a) interprets Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 (this code sections specifically
mentions “outside income”); (7) the last sentence of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a)(1) requires the separate calculation to determine the amount of tax owed
on the source income (the first sentence of the second paragraph of
the Regulation is not referring to the same thing); (8) he does not know what the
first sentence of the second paragraph of the Regulation is interpreting; and (9)
the Instructions for AR1000TC do not override a regulation or a statute.

STATEMENT OF FACTS
The Taxpayer is an Arkansas resident who is employed as a
sales manager for . For the years at
issue, in addition to his employment income, the Taxpayer also
reported gambling income. As a resident of Arkansas,
during these years, the nearest casinos to the Taxpayer were in
For this reason, the Taxpayer gambled almost
exclusively in
Since he earned source income, the Taxpayer,
through his CPA, , filed a
nonresident income tax return (Form 511NR) and paid
state income tax. The amount of income tax
paid each year was calculated in accordance with law as
follows:
1. The Taxpayer determined his source
income.
2. The Taxpayer determined his Federal adjusted gross
income ("AGI").
3. The Taxpayer subtracted his itemized deductions and
exemptions from his Federal AGI to determine his
net taxable income ("NTI"). See Lines 7 through 14, Form
. See also Instructions for Lines 7 through 14 for Form
.
4. The Taxpayer calculated his income tax
based on the tax table. See Line 15, Form .
See also Instructions for Line 15 for Form .
5. The Taxpayer multiplied his income tax by
a fraction, the numerator of which was the Taxpayer's
source income and the denominator of which was
the Taxpayer's Federal AGI. The product was the amount of
income tax.
(See tax returns attached as Exhibit 3.) As a result, the
Taxpayer only paid income tax on the portion of his total
income represented by his source income. See Lines 18
16

and 19, Form . See also Instructions for Lines 18 and 19 for
Form .
As an Arkansas resident in the years at issue, the Taxpayer
filed an Arkansas income tax return for a full year resident (Form
1000F) and paid Arkansas state income tax. The amount of
Arkansas income tax paid each year was calculated as follows:
1. The Taxpayer determined his total income. See Line
21, Form 1000F. See also Instructions for Line 21 for Form
1000F.
2. The Taxpayer determined his Arkansas AGI. See Line
23, Form 1000F. See also Instructions for Line 23 for Form
1000F.
3. The Taxpayer subtracted his itemized deductions
from his Arkansas AGI to determine his Arkansas NTI.
4. The Taxpayer calculated his Arkansas income tax
based on the Arkansas tax table.
5. The Taxpayer calculated his Other State Tax Credit
using Form 1000TC.
6. The Taxpayer subtracted his Other State Tax Credit
and other tax credits to determine his net Arkansas tax.
(See Arkansas tax returns attached as Exhibit 4.)
In each of the preceding tax return preparation processes,
followed the applicable instructions for preparing the
return, including the instructions for Form AR1000TC. On June
12, 2019, Kevin Melson, Tax Auditor for the DFA ("Mr. Melson"),
sent the Taxpayer ETAs for tax years 2013 through 2018 (attached).

ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
Arkansas imposes its income tax on the entire income earned
by Arkansas residents regardless of where the income is earned.
See Ark. Code Ann§ 26-51-201 (Supp. 2017). As a result, Arkansas
residents deriving income from other states may have income tax
imposed both by Arkansas and by the state where the income was
earned. Arkansas addresses the possibility of double taxation by
granting a credit to Arkansas residents against their Arkansas
income tax liability for income tax paid to the state where the
income was earned. That credit is found in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a)(1).
The credit for taxes paid to another state may be taken only
for that portion of the taxpayer's income that is subject to tax in
both states. However, the amount of credit that may be taken for
tax paid to the other state may not exceed the amount of Arkansas
income tax imposed on that income subject to tax in both states.
Taxpayer had significant source income from
gambling winnings during the tax years in question. As an
Arkansas resident, Taxpayer is required to report his income from
those gambling winnings on his Arkansas income tax return and
may claim an itemized deduction under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-424
for any gambling losses incurred during that same year. Those
deductible gambling losses may not exceed the gambling winnings
for that year.
Taxpayer's gambling winnings are also subject to income tax
in . To prevent double taxation, Taxpayer is allowed an
Arkansas income tax credit for the income tax paid to on
those winnings. However, Taxpayer claimed a credit for taxes paid
to for the years in question that exceeded the Arkansas

because the amount of the tax credits claimed was contrary to
Arkansas law for the reasons explained below.
1. Arkansas Code Annotated § 26-51-504(a)(1) limits the
credit for taxes paid to other states to no more than the
Arkansas income tax due on the item of income subject
to tax in both states.
The language of Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) regarding
the credit against the Arkansas income tax for taxes paid to another
state on income subject to tax in both states contains three subparts
with regard to calculating the amount of credit. These subparts are:
26

• The tax shall first be computed as if all of the income of the
resident were derived from sources within the State of
Arkansas;
• A credit shall then be given on the tax as so computed, for
the amount of income tax actually owed by the resident for
the year to any other state or territory on account of income
from property owned or business transacted in the other
state or territory;
• The credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on the
outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and
calculated at Arkansas income tax rates.
The third bullet point contains the limitation at issue in this case.
This limitation requires a taxpayer to separately determine the
Arkansas income tax due on the other state income and limits the
Arkansas credit to the amount of Arkansas tax due on that other
state income.
In their publication State Taxation Vol. II (3rd Ed. 2003),
professors Jerome R. Hellerstein and Walter Hellerstein at
¶20.10[1] discuss the limitations imposed by states when providing
a credit to its residents for income taxes paid to other states. They
explain that states generally limit the amount of credit a taxpayer
may claim in two ways. First, states provide that the credit allowed
by the resident state is limited to only the tax paid to the other state
on income subject to tax in both states. This limitation is clearly
articulated in the language of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1)
referenced in the second bullet point above. Second, the credit for
tax paid on the out-of-state income may not exceed the tax imposed
on that same income by the resident state. They further explain
that this second limitation is typically determined in one of the
following ways:
1. Multiplying the resident's state tax liability by the ratio
of income taxed by the other state to the resident's taxable
income;
2. Multiplying the income taxed by both states by the
resident state rate on such income; or
3. Determining the difference between the resident tax
calculated by first including and then excluding the income
subject to tax in both states.
Professors Hellerstein and Hellerstein then analyze the effects of
these three methods as follows:
27

Method 1 limits the credit to a tax calculated based on the
average tax rate applied to the resident's income. Method 2
limits the credit to a tax calculated as if the income being
taxed by the other state were the first dollars earned by the
taxpayer (i.e. at the lowest marginal rates to which such
income could be subjected).
Method 3 limits the credit to a tax calculated as if the
income being taxed by the other state were the last dollars
earned by the taxpayer (i.e. at the highest marginal rates to
which such income could be subjected).
The last sentence of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1),

In its analysis the Court stated:
The objective of the above-quoted statutory provisions was
to avoid the double taxation of the same income by
providing a credit against New Jersey gross income tax for
tax paid to another jurisdiction on the same income. The
limitation on the credit provides a formula which separates
such taxed foreign income from New Jersey taxable
income. See Ambrose v. Tax. Division Director, 198
N.J.Super. 546, 487 A.2d 1274 (App.Div.1984); Sorenson v.
Tax. Division Director, 184 N.J Super. 393, 2 N.J.Tax 470,
446 A.2d 213 (Tax Ct.1981). In those cases, the issues
involved the effect on the credit when New York based
income was not taxed by New York State. Here, the issue

involves the effect on the credit when New York based
income is taxed by New York State and not by New Jersey.
The Court then determined that the credit for tax paid to the other
state was only available for income subject to income tax by both
states. The Court concluded by stating:
The literal language of N.J.S.A. 54A:4-1(b) states that the
maximum credit "shall not exceed the proportion of the tax
otherwise due under the act that the amount of taxpayers'
income subject to tax by the other jurisdiction bears to his
entire New Jersey income." That language could literally be
interpreted to permit the total of taxpayers' New York
income, whether or not taxed by New Jersey, to be included
in the numerator. However, section (b) must be read in
conjunction with section (a). Section (a) clearly restricts
the credit to foreign taxed income which is also taxed by
New Jersey. To include in the maximum credit factor the
foreign income which was not taxed by New Jersey would
be at variance with the provisions of section (a) and would
reach the absurd result of having New Jersey grant a credit
against its tax on New Jersey income on the basis that a
resident taxpayer had paid a tax to a foreign jurisdiction on
income which was not taxable in New Jersey.

compliance with Arkansas law, the Taxpayer claimed a credit for
the lesser of taxes actually owed to or his total tax
liability in Arkansas. The DFA disallowed the Taxpayer's claim for a
tax credit for taxes paid to ; however, such disallowance
is not supported by Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 or by Arkansas
Individual Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a).
In its opening brief, the DFA has supplied secondary sources
and out-of-state court decisions interpreting different statutes (i.e.,
statutes that are not Arkansas statutes) in an attempt to read
limitations into the Arkansas law that are simply not provided in
any Arkansas law. In order to sustain the DFA' s disallowance, this
Office of Hearings and Appeals would have to essentially amend
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 by reading into it additional limitations
and steps to the calculation of the Other State Tax Credit that are
not provided for in the applicable statute and regulation.
Amending a statute is not appropriate for this Office and is a matter
that should be left for the Arkansas General Assembly. For these
reasons, the DFA's disallowance of the credit must be overturned.
C. TAXPAYER’S ARGUMENTS
I. A STRICT READING OF ARK. CODE ANN. §26-51-
504 REQUIRES THE TAXPAYER’S CLAIMS FOR OTHER
STATE TAX CREDITS BE REINSTATED.
Despite not being mentioned in the DFA's opening brief, Mr.
Melson's only cited authority in the ETAs to support the
disallowance of the Other State Tax Credit is Arkansas Individual
Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). The relevant language of
this regulation is as follows:
When the gross income of an Arkansas resident includes
income derived from sources outside the State of Arkansas,
such as property or business activity, the Arkansas income
tax liability shall first be computed as if all of the Arkansas
resident's income was derived from sources within the State
of Arkansas. However, a credit shall be allowed
against the resident's Arkansas income tax liability
in the amount of any income tax actually owed by
the resident for the tax year at issue to any other
state or territory.
35

Any credit given shall not be allowed to exceed what the
tax would be on all the Arkansas resident's
income, from wherever derived, if such tax was
calculated using Arkansas income tax rates. No credit
shall be allowed against the resident's Arkansas income
tax liability unless the resident can clearly show that he or
she would be subject to double taxation on a portion of his
or her income unless the credit is allowed.
Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a)
(emphasis added). Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation §
1.26-51-504(a) interprets Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504, which
provides in relevant part:
(1) For the purpose of ascertaining the income tax due by an
individual resident of Arkansas whose gross income
includes income derived from property located outside the
State of Arkansas, or from business transacted outside the
State of Arkansas, the tax shall first be computed as if all of
the income of the resident were derived from sources
within the State of Arkansas, but a credit shall then be
given on the tax as so computed, for the amount of income
tax actually owed by the resident for the year to any other
state or territory on account of income from property
owned or business transacted in the other state or territory.
However, credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on
the outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and
calculated at Arkansas income tax rates. (Emphasis added)
The predecessor to Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504, was codified
from Act 162 of 1943 (the "Act"). The Act is captioned as:
AN ACT to Prevent Double State Income Taxation of
Individual Residents of Arkansas. Section 1 of the Act
provides that when the gross income of an Arkansas
resident includes income derived from property outside the
State or business transacted outside the State, the Arkansas
tax shall be first computed as if all the income were derived
from inside the State; and then a credit shall be given
for the amount of income tax owed by the Arkansas
resident to the State or Territory from which such
income has been received by the taxpayer.
Morley v. Pills, 217 Ark. 755,233 S.W.2d 539, footnote 1 (1950)
(emphasis added). The current version of the statute can be broken
down into three parts: (1) when the credit applies, (2) the amount of
the credit, and (3) the limitation of the credit. These parts are

ARGUMENT
(a) The Department correctly assessed tax of because
the Taxpayer underreported its taxable sales, charged
additional taxes that it did not remit, and failed to remit use tax
on out of state purchases.
1. The Taxpayer received credit for all sales tax remitted to the
Department.
The Taxpayer's recordkeeping, or lack thereof, made it impossible
to tie any one invoice to the taxable sales reported to the
Department on its monthly sales tax report. Therefore, the
reported taxable sales were subtracted from the taxable sales as
determined by the audit. This approach allowed the Taxpayer to
receive credit for all sales tax remitted to the Department and was
reasonable.
2. The Department reasonably estimated the sales tax due in
tax years 2014, 2015, 2016, and 2017.
Taxpayers are required to maintain suitable records to prove the
amount of tax due or the accuracy of a return. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-
18-506(a) (Repl. 2020). In the absence of those records, the
Department is entitled to estimate an assessment based on the
records available. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-506(d) (Repl. 2020).
The burden of refuting the reasonableness of that estimate is on the
Taxpayer. Id.

The Taxpayer failed to maintain a comprehensive set of invoices for
tax years 2014, 2015, 2016, and 2017.[Footnote 5 stated that, “The
Taxpayer was able to provide a Quick Books listing for the last six
months of 2017 but that listing was not supported by a complete set
of invoices and did not address the first half of 2017. For example,
only two invoices were provided for May 2017.”] The auditor
employed a reasonable estimate to assess additional taxable sales
for each of these periods. She used the total gross sales as reported
on the Taxpayer's income tax returns to generate total sales by
month and gave credit for taxable sales reported to the Department.
The amount of any invoice provided for those tax periods was also
subtracted for each month. The Taxpayer's income tax returns are
documents completed by the Taxpayer or its representative and are
sworn to be accurate when submitted to the Department. This
approach was reasonable because it was based on numbers
provided by the Taxpayer on official tax documents.
The Taxpayer's protest contends that this approach was not
reasonable because it resulted in a higher percentage of sales being
deemed taxable during periods without records than during the
years where records were available (2018, 2019, and 2020). This
difference resulted from the Taxpayer's business function changing
during the audit period. Based on the limited invoices available for
the estimated periods, it appears the Taxpayer was performing
almost entirely taxable vehicle related services. Around February
2018, the Taxpayer's main business function became selling its
services to was a direct pay permit holder and
the Taxpayer would not have been obligated to collect or remit sales
tax on services sold to When put in the context of the
Taxpayer's changing business model, the discrepancy in the
percentage of income deemed taxable is reasonable.
3. The Department correctly charged tax on the invoices
reflected in Basis Code 2.
Arkansas imposes a sales tax on transactions involving the
alteration, replacement, and repair of motor vehicles, motors, tires,
electrical appliances and devices, machinery, and mechanical tools.
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-301 (Repl. 2020). Other taxable services
include cleaning, lawn care, storing a motor vehicle, wrecker and
towing services, collection and disposal of solid wastes, and
cleaning of parking lots. Id.; Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-316 (Repl.
2020). Sales of tangible personal property are taxable. Ark. Code
Ann.§ 26-52-301(1)(A) (Repl. 2020).
All of the invoices marked as Basis Code 2 were for the sale of

taxable services or tangible personal property. Exhibit C.
Therefore, these transactions are taxable. If the Taxpayer claims
some exemption applies, it bears the burden of proving that

4. The Department correctly assessed an additional amount
for excessive taxes collected by the Taxpayer under the color
of the State's authority but not remitted to the Department.
A taxpayer who collects tax in excess of what is required by law
must remit to the Department the sums collected. See Cook v.
Sears-Roebuck & Co., 212 Ark. 308, 206 S.W.2d 20 (1947). Where
a tax collector is acting under the power and authority of a sales tax
permit and that tax collector collects an amount under the power
and authority of that permit, that money either belongs to the State
or the customer from whom the tax was collected. Id. 212 Ark. at
312, 206 S.W.2d at 22. In no scenario does it belong to the business
acting as the tax collector. Id.
The state sales tax rate is 6.5%. Localities are entitled to charge
additional sales tax, but those sales taxes are administered and
collected at the state level by the Department. Here, the invoices
provided by the Taxpayer indicate that it was routinely charging
more tax than was imposed by the state and locality. Exhibits C &
N. This additional amount was charged under the label “tax.” It
was clearly collected under the power and authority of the
Taxpayer's sales tax permit.
A reasonable customer would expect the money collected under the
label "tax" to be collected and remitted to the State. It would not
expect the Taxpayer to retain some of the tax while remitting only a
portion to the State. The additional charge was not part of the
bargain struck between the Taxpayer and its customers. The
Department is within its rights under Sears-Roebuck & Co., 212
Ark. 308, 206 S.W.2d 20 to collect this additional amount of tax
charged by the Taxpayer to its customers.
For years where a complete set of invoices were available, the
additional tax charged was calculated based on those invoices.
Where incomplete invoices were provided, the Department was
entitled to employ a reasonable estimation, which it did by
calculating the additional tax charged as 1% of the additional total
sales assessed under Basis Code 3 for each month. See Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-18-506(d) (Rep1. 2020).

6. The Department correctly assessed use tax on purchases
made by the Taxpayer.
Where tangible personal property "is purchased for use or
consumption in Arkansas from a seller in another state . . . such sale
is subject to Arkansas compensating use tax." Arkansas Gross
Receipts Tax Rule GR-5(C)(2). The Arkansas customer must remit
compensating use tax to the Department if the out of state seller
fails to collect Arkansas' tax. Id. In the event the Arkansas
customer pays sales or use tax to another state, he is entitled to full
credit for that tax paid against any use tax owed to Arkansas or any
13

subdivision thereof. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-5-101 (Art. V) (Repl.
2020); Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax Rule GR-5(C)(2).
The Taxpayer produced several invoices for out of state purchases
that refelcted no tax was charged by the out of state vendor. These
items, t-shirts, hats, tools, and building materials, were purchased
for use or consumption in Arkansas. Therefore, use tax was
properly assessed on these items.
The Taxpayer's depreciation schedule indicated that it purchased
equipment during the audit period. These items were used at the
Taxpayer's business in Arkansas. The Taxpayer did not maintain
invoices regarding those purchases. The Department assessed use

The burden of proof applied to matters of fact and evidence,
whether placed on the taxpayer or the state in controversies
regarding the application of a state tax law shall be by
preponderance of the evidence.
A preponderance of the evidence means the greater weight of the evidence.
Chandler v. Baker, 16 Ark. App. 253, 700 S.W.2d 378 (1985). In Edmisten v. Bull
Shoals Landing, 2014 Ark. 89, at 12-13, 432 S.W.3d 25, 33, the Arkansas Supreme
Court explained:
A preponderance of the evidence is “not necessarily established by
the greater number of witnesses testifying to a fact but by evidence
that has the most convincing force; superior evidentiary weight
that, though not sufficient to free the mind wholly from all
reasonable doubt, is still sufficient to incline a fair and impartial
mind to one side of the issue rather than the other.
The Department bears the burden of proving that the tax law applies to an
item or service sought to be taxed, and a taxpayer bears the burden of proving
entitlement to a tax exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(d) (Repl. 2020).
Statutes imposing a tax or providing a tax exemption, deduction, or credit
must be reasonably and strictly construed in limitation of their application,
giving the words their plain and ordinary meaning. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(a), (b), and (e) (Repl. 2020).
If a well-founded doubt exists with respect to the application of a statute
imposing a tax or providing a tax exemption, deduction, or credit, the doubt must
be resolved against the application of the tax, exemption, deduction, or credit.
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(f)(2) (Repl. 2020).

the evidence supports a finding that the Taxpayer charged some of its customers
a tax rate in excess of the rate required by the state and the applicable locality.
With respect to this issue (Basis Code 1), the Department contended that:
. . . the Taxpayer charged its customers a tax rate in excess of that
required by the state and locality. The Department assessed the
Taxpayer for the additional amounts collected from its customers
because this additional money was collected under the color of the
State's authority and the Taxpayer was not entitled to retain those
amounts. The additional amounts assessed are reflected in column

The Taxpayer did not refute those contentions. In Cook v. Sears-Roebuck
& Co., 212 Ark. 308, 206 S.W.2d 20 (1947), the Arkansas Supreme Court
addressed the issue of whether a vendor may retain proceeds that it believed were
improperly collected. Sears operated mail order desks whose sales were
ultimately approved and shipped from out of state. Sears originally collected and
remitted tax on the mail order sales but, in January 1945, Sears continued to
27 See Department’s Answers to Information Request – P. 2.
32

collect the tax from its mail order customers but did not remit the tax to the
Department. In July 1945, the Department assessed Sears for the taxes collected
but not remitted on its mail order sales. On appeal, Sears argued that Arkansas
Sales Tax did not apply to the mail order transactions because the sales were
completed out of state, and, consequently, it should not be required to remit the
proceeds to the Department. Id. at 320, 206 S.W.2d at 26. When discussing the
ownership of the tax proceeds, the Arkansas Supreme Court noted: “Either, it
belongs to the State, or it belongs to the persons who paid the taxes to Sears. At
all events, it is not Sears' money.” Id. at 312, 206 S.W.2d at 22. The Arkansas
Supreme Court ultimately concluded “that Sears' status under our Tax Act is that
of a tax collector, and that the rule against unjust enrichment is a bar to Sears'
effort to recover (or retain) the tax which Sears collected from its customers
under this Tax Act.” Id. at 319-320, 206 S.W.2d at 26. The Arkansas Supreme
further concluded that it was not a valid defense to the assessment for Sears to
argue that the taxes it collected and retained should not have been collected. Id.
at 320, 206 S.W.2d at 26. Under the Sears Roebuck case, it is evident that, if the
Taxpayer collected sales tax from its customers, those proceeds must be remitted
to the Department even if the tax was collected on nontaxable transactions.
The Department has statutory authority to “[a]udit and properly

IV.
A withdrawal from stock is subject to tax under Arkansas Gross Receipts
Tax Rule GR-18(D). In Weiss v. Central Flying Service, Inc., 326 Ark. 685, 934
S.W.2d 211 (1996), the Arkansas Supreme Court addressed the taxability of a
withdrawal from stock and stated, in pertinent part, as follows:
. . . With respect to a purchaser regularly engaged in the business of
reselling items purchased, a sale for resale exemption is provided
which relieves him of paying tax on such purchases. See Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-52-401(12)(A) (Supp. 1995). However, if that purchaser
withdraws and uses an item from his inventory rather than resell it,
such an event constitutes a withdrawal from stock and the
purchaser is deemed the consumer. Georgia Pacific Corp. v. Lay,
242 Ark. 428, 413 S.W.2d 868 (1967). Items withdrawn from stock
become subject to gross receipts tax, usually based on the purchase
price of the items used. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-103(a)(4) (Supp.
1995). Once an item is withdrawn from stock, the protection of the
resale exemption is lost, and the tax is due on or before the 20th of
the month following the month in which the items or goods were
withdrawn. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-501 (Supp. 1995).

Procedural Disputes and Objections
The parties made several objections regarding the pre-hearing production
of documents (or data) and the post-audit submission of documents. Those
issues really involve audit disputes more so than legal controversies. Similar
cases in the past have focused on the authority vested in the Office of Hearings
and Appeals. In a Revision Decision issued in May of 2019, the Commissioner of
Revenues delineated the authority of the Office of Hearings and Appeals and held
that:
42

The duties of a hearing officer appointed by the Department are
limited to reviewing written protests and making written findings
as to the applicability of a proposed assessment or denial of a claim
for refund. Accordingly, it is outside the scope of the duties of the
hearing officer to provide taxpayers with guidance concerning the
existence of programs to request a waiver of interest or penalties.
Given the parameter of duties outlined above, it would be outside the
scope of the duties of a hearing officer to determine the weight or relevance of
documents not reviewed during an audit (Taxpayer Exhibit A) or to order a re-
audit of a matter submitted for consideration based on disputes regarding the
production of documents (or data).

Subject to the limitation in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-405(d)(1)(C) (Repl.

State’s tax dollars. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-508 (Repl. 2020). Under the
facts and circumstances of this case, a penalty was properly imposed on the sales
tax assessment under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-208 (Repl. 2020). No penalty was
imposed on the use tax assessment.

The Department’s Answers to Information Request provided, in pertinent

(4) State the issue(s) (points of protest).
Whether the assessment of income tax and the interest imposed on

Department's regulation regarding granter trusts is invalid, and (4)
imposition of a tax without legislative authority constitutes an
illegal exaction under Arkansas's constitution.
(5) Discuss in detail the facts upon which you rely to
support your case.
Both taxpayers were investors in

Trust" (the
"Trust"). Exhibit 1. The trustee of the trust was
, a company located in . On the same day the trust
agreement was signed, each taxpayer irrevocably transferred to the

with principal offices in . The

Paragraph 7(b) of the Trust states: "Notwithstanding the powers

retain the ability . . . [t]o control the investments of the Trust, either
by directing investments or reinvestments or by vetoing proposed

Paragraph 7(c) of the Trust states: "Notwithstanding the powers

Grantors retain the ability . . . [t]o reaquire or exchange any

Arkansas imposes income tax on every resident, individual, trust, or
estate. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201. Despite this broad language,
income tax would not be due when a grantor of a trust is not the
owner of property subject to a trust. Therefore, the Department
promulgated Rule 4.26-51-102 of its Comprehensive Individual
Income Tax Regulations to clarify when a grantor of a trust should
be deemed the owner of property subject to a trust. Rule 4.26-51-
102 states "A trust whereby the grantor retains control over the
income or corpus (trust property) or both, to such an extent that the
granter will be treated as the owner of the property and its income
for income tax purposes. The general result is that the income from
a grantor trust is taxable to the grantor, as "owner" of the trust, and
not to the fiduciary. In determining whether a trust is a grantor
trust, the grantor's degree of control over the trust must be
analyzed." Rule 4.26-51- 102 further instructs to look to " IRC Sec.
671 et seq." for guidance on this question.
26 U.S.C. § 675(4) states, "The granter shall be treated as the owner
of any portion of a trust in respect of which . . . [a] power of
administration is exercisable in a nonfiduciary capacity by any
person without the approval or consent of any person in a fiduciary
capacity. For purposes of this paragraph, the term "power of
administration" means any one or more of the following powers:
(A) a power to vote or direct the voting of stock or other securities
of a corporation in which the holdings of the grantor and the trust
are significant from the viewpoint of voting control; (B) a power
to control the investment of the trust funds either by
directing investments or reinvestments, or by vetoing
proposed investments or reinvestments, to the extent that
the trust funds consist of stocks or securities of
corporations in which the holdings of the grantor and the
trust are significant from the viewpoint of voting control;
or (C) a power to reacquire the trust corpus by
substituting other property of an equivalent value.
(emphasis added).
3

The taxpayers have never disputed that federal law required them
to be treated as the owners of the trust property. In fact, the
taxpayer reported the income on their 2016 federal return. Exhibit
3. Because the taxpayers clearly believe that for federal income tax
purposes they fall within the language of 26 U.S.C. § 675(4), the
only question that remains is whether they fall within the language
of 26 U.S.C. § 675(4) for Arkansas Income Tax purposes.
For these reasons, the taxpayers cannot claim that the Department
has not met its burden of proof. The Arkansas General Assembly
has clearly stated that trust income is subject to tax. Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-51-201. The Department has issued a rule to clarify when the
grantor of a trust should be treated as the owner of the property
subject to trust. The trust agreement retained in its grantors the
power to control its investments and to substitute trust corpus
property. Because of this retention of power, the taxpayers are to
be treated as the owners of the trust. Therefore, the trust gains they
reported on their 2016 federal income tax return are subject to tax
in Arkansas.
For the same reasons, the taxpayer's next two arguments (i.e. that
Arkansas has not enacted any law regarding taxation of grantor
trusts and the Department's regulation regarding grantor trusts is

In 2015, the Arkansas General Assembly revisited the burden
of proof that applies to the interpretation of the Arkansas tax laws.
See, gen. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313. When the meaning of a state
tax law is in controversy, the burden of establishing the proper
construction of the statute is upon the party claiming application of
the tax. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(d). Here, that burden is placed
upon the state, which is acting by and through the DFA. Where the
state seeks to impose a tax under the terms of a state tax law, then
the statute imposing the tax must be strictly construed in limitation
of the imposition of the tax. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(a).
Where, as here, the Taxpayers are not claiming an exemption
from a tax, but rather claiming that a tax could not be levied upon
the Taxpayers, the DFA has the burden of proving the propriety of
the tax, and all doubts and ambiguities are resolved in favor of the
Taxpayers. See id. See also Leathers v. A & B Dirt Movers, Inc.,
311 Ark. 320, 325, 844 S.W.2d 314, 216 (1992); Dunhill
Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. State, 295 Ark. 483, 749 S.W.2d 666
(1988); Central and Southern Co. v. Weiss, 339 Ark. 76, 3 S.W.3d
294 (1999). Separate from the burden that applies to the
application and interpretation of Arkansas' tax laws, when it comes
to matters of fact and evidence, the burden of proof is that of a
preponderance of the evidence. Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-52-313(c).
Thus, the DFA has the burden of proof to show by a
preponderance of the evidence that under its proper construction, a
law exists which taxes these Taxpayers on the 2016 income of the
Trust. The law must be strictly construed to limit any
imposition of tax, and all doubts and ambiguities about that law
must be resolved in favor of the Taxpayers. If, after consideration
of same, a well-founded doubt still exists as to the meaning of a
statute imposing a tax, the rule of strict construction requires that
the doubt be resolved against the tax and in favor of the Taxpayers.
Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-52-313(f)(2).

implement and clarify the Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929
(emphasis provided). By Ark. Code Ann. § 19-1-208, the General
Assembly expressly limited the power of the Director of the DFA
when it comes to issuing regulations, mandating that such rules and
regulations shall not be inconsistent with the law. However, the
DFA here asserts that the general taxing statute, Ark. Code Ann. §
26-51-201, permits the DFA to "further define" what is taxed by the
statute. In doing so the DFA instead attempts to legislate new
taxing powers over matters not taxed by the General Assembly in
the Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929.
There are at least two problems with the DFA's approach:
First, Regulation 4.26-51-102 is promulgated under Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-51-102, which is a definitional statute that does not even define
much less mention grantor trusts. There simply is no "existing law"
i.e., no Arkansas Code provision (including Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
102) that Regulation 4.26-51-102 is attempting to implement and
clarify. Rather, Regulation 4.26-51-102 is a wholly legislative effort
by the DFA to adopt laws to tax granter trusts in Arkansas where
such law has never been adopted by the Arkansas General
Assembly.
Second, this effort by the DFA to enact laws via regulation
violates the separation-of-powers doctrine and cannot stand. An
agency does not have the authority to extend its power or reach in
the absence of a statutory mandate. Arkansas State Board of
Election Comm'rs v. Pulaski Cty. Election Comm'n, 437 S.W.3d 80,
83 (Ark. 2014). The functions belonging to one department may
not be usurped by the other, nor may the right to exercise such
authority be delegated. Oates v. Rogers, 144 S.W.2d 457, 458 (Ark.
1940). To be clear, under the separation-of-powers doctrine, the
functions of the legislature must be exercised by the legislature
alone. Walden v. Hart, 243 Ark. 650, 652 (Ark. 1967).
As discussed by the Arkansas Supreme Court in Federal
Express Corp. v. Skelton, 265 Ark. 187, 198, 578 S.W.2d 1, 7 (1979)
our government is composed of three separate, independent
branches: the legislative, the executive, and the judicial. Each
branch has certain specified powers delegated to it. Id. The

legislative branch of our state government has the power and the
responsibility to proclaim the law through statutory enactments.
Id. The judicial branch has the power and the responsibility to
interpret the legislative enactments. Id. The executive branch has
the power and the responsibility to enforce the laws as enacted and
interpreted by the other two branches. Id.
The Arkansas Supreme Court teaches that the separation-of-
powers doctrine is a basic principle upon which our state
government is founded, and one which must not be violated or
abridged. Id. That proscription bars the DFA from stepping in to

Standard of Proof
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(c) (Supp. 2019) provides, in pertinent part, as
follows:
The burden of proof applied to matters of fact and evidence,
whether placed on the taxpayer or the state in controversies
regarding the application of a state tax law shall be by
preponderance of the evidence.

A preponderance of the evidence means the greater weight of the evidence.
Chandler v. Baker, 16 Ark. App. 253, 700 S.W.2d 378 (1985). In Edmisten v. Bull
Shoals Landing, 2014 Ark. 89, at 12-13, 432 S.W.3d 25, 33, the Arkansas Supreme
Court explained:
A preponderance of the evidence is “not necessarily established by the
greater number of witnesses testifying to a fact but by evidence that has
the most convincing force; superior evidentiary weight that, though not
sufficient to free the mind wholly from all reasonable doubt, is still
sufficient to incline a fair and impartial mind to one side of the issue
rather than the other.
The Department bears the burden of proving that the tax law applies to an
item or service sought to be taxed, and a taxpayer bears the burden of proving
entitlement to a tax exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(d) (Supp. 2019). Statutes imposing a tax or providing a tax exemption,
deduction, or credit must be reasonably and strictly construed in limitation of
their application, giving the words their plain and ordinary meaning. Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-18-313(a), (b), and (e) (Supp. 2019). If a well-founded doubt exists
with respect to the application of a statute imposing a tax or providing a tax
exemption, deduction, or credit, the doubt must be resolved against the
application of the tax, exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(f)(2) (Supp. 2019).

I. The Director Has the Authority to Promulgate the
Grantor Trust Rules in Rule 4.26-51-102 of the
Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Regulations.
When the Arkansas General Assembly chose the language of the
Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929, it chose extraordinarily broad
language. It chose to impose its income tax on " every resident,
individual, trust, or estate." Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201(a)
(emphasis added). Then, it defined gross income to include
"[g]ains or profits and income derived from any source whatever."
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404(a)(1)(E) (emphasis added). Somewhat
more specifically, it defined gross income to include "[g]ains,
profits, and income derived from dealings in property, whether real
or personal, growing out of the ownership of, use of, or interest in
the property." § 404(a)(1)(C). But even this more specific language
left open numerous obvious, yet unanswered questions.
In particular, when the Arkansas General Assembly set forth the
definition of "gross income" in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404, it did
not state what interests in a property are sufficient to require an
individual to report gains on the property as gross income. Clearly,
not any interest in a property is sufficient, but the General
Assembly has never drawn the line - a line that unquestionably
must be drawn somewhere.
Instead, the Arkansas General Assembly passed Act 401 of 1979,
which gave the Director of the Department of Finance
correspondingly broad authority to promulgate necessary rules for
the administration of the Individual Income Tax. See Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-301 (a)(1). Out of this authority and based on the
need to draw this line, the Director of the Department of Finance
and Administration ("Director") promulgated Rule 4.26-51-102 of
the Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Rules (the "Rule"),
which provides a reasonable answer to the specific question of what
interests in trust property are sufficient to subject gains on the trust
property to the definition of gross income.
For the purpose of setting forth a basis upon which to determine
what interests in a property are sufficient to require an individual to
report gains on the property as gross income, the Rule centers its
analysis around one patently reasonable consideration: control. As
it pertains to the assessment in question, the income from a grantor
trust - defined as "[a] trust whereby the grantor retains control over
the income or corpus (trust property) or both, to such an extent that
the grantor will be treated as the owner of the property and its
income for income tax purposes" - is taxable to the grantor, as
"owner" of the trust, and not to the fiduciary. Id. In determining
36

whether a trust is a grantor trust, the Rule states that the grantor's
degree of control over the trust must be analyzed. Id. To aid in this
analysis, the Rule utilizes the circumstances described in IRC § 671
et. seq. to identify when the grantor has retained such control.
Those circumstances are discussed in Part II of this Post-Hearing
Brief.
The grantor trust rules in Rule 4.26-51-102 are both reasonable and
do not run contrary to a statute. See McLane Co., Inc. v. Weiss, 332
Ark. 284, 965 S.W.2d 109 (1998) ("an agency has no right to
promulgate a rule or regulation contrary to a statute"). As stated,
the Arkansas General Assembly has not defined what constitutes a
sufficient interest nor has it defined what constitutes ownership of
property for income tax purposes. That determining the sufficiency
of the interest in a property is an essential question in determining
the applicability of the tax was not seriously challenged in the
hearing.
Further, control over the trust property is a reasonable basis for
evaluating whether an interest in a property is sufficient. While the
Taxpayers are correct that "when the state seeks to impose a tax
under the terms of a state tax law, then the statute imposing the tax
shall be strictly construed in limitation of the imposition of the tax,"
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313, the Director's authority to promulgate
the Rule that is necessary to clarify Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-404
comes from Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301, which does not itself
impose a tax. For that reason, the Department's interpretation of §
301 should be highly persuasive, and it should be upheld unless it is
"clearly wrong." See Macsteel, Parnell Consultants v. Ar. Ok. Gas
Corp., 363 Ark. 22, 210 S.W.3d 878 (2005). A court will not
attempt to substitute its judgment for that of the administrative
agency. Arkansas Health Services Commission v. Regional Care
Facilities, Inc., 351 Ark. 331, 338, 93 S.W.3d 672 (2002).
To prohibit the Department - for the reasons the Taxpayers state -
from promulgating such common-sense rules such as Rule 4.26-51-
102 would have terrible consequences. For instance, the
Department could not treat the grantor of a revocable trust as the
owner of the trust's property, which CIITR 7.26-51-102 properly
directs as a matter of common sense, despite not originating in
statute. . . ..
Finally, the Taxpayers argued in their hearing that the Rule
invalidly adopted § 675 of the Internal Revenue Code because the
Director did not specify the year of the section's existence the Rule
was referring to. In so doing, the Taxpayers presumably argue that
rulemaking power has unconstitutionally been delegated to the
37

United States Congress.
This argument is misplaced for two reasons. First, in the twenty-
one years since the Rule at the heart of this assessment was
promulgated, Congress has not actually amended § 675. The
concern that one would not know what version of § 675 to apply is a
hypothetical problem. Second, the Taxpayer's argument leaves
intact the essential and operative parts of the Rule. The fact that a
portion of a regulation is void does not invalidate the whole
regulation where such portion is distinctly separable from the
remainder which in itself contains the essentials of a complete
regulation. McLane Co., Inc. v. Weiss, 332 Ark. 284, 965 S.W.2d
109 (1998). The essential parts of the Rule are (1) that a trust is
taxable to the grantor when the grantor retains control over the
income or corpus (trust property) or both to such an extent that the
grantor will be treated as the owner of the property and its income
for income tax purposes and (2) that in determining whether a trust
is a grantor trust, the grantor's degree of control over the trust must
be analyzed. These two statements themselves do not delegate any
authority. Even if the Rule made no explicit reference to the federal
statutes at IRC § 671 et. seq., their analytical framework on the
question of control over trust property would still be relevant.
The Rule being challenged in this assessment answers questions left
unanswered by the Arkansas General Assembly, is within the
Director's broad authority to promulgate necessary rules, is not
contrary to statute, is reasonable, and does not unconstitutionally
delegate legislative authority.
For these reasons, the Director of the Department of Finance and
Administration has the authority to promulgate Rule 4.26-51-102 of
the Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Regulations.

A. A Regulation is not Valid Even if it is “Reasonable”
But is “Inconsistent With the Law.”
The DFA argues that it had the authority to promulgate
Regulation 4.26-51-102 because that Regulation is "reasonable."
Despite its argument to the contrary, the DFA cannot promulgate
regulations inconsistent with Arkansas law under an argument of
"reasonableness," because to do so completely ignores the statutory
requirement that a regulation issued by the Director must both be
reasonable and not inconsistent with the law. Ark. Code Ann.§ 19-
1-208. In its Post-Hearing Brief, the DFA cites to McLane Co., Inc.
v. Weiss, 332 Ark. 284, 965 S.W.2d 109 (1998) for the proposition
that an agency has no right to promulgate a rule or regulation
contrary to a statute. That is indeed a true statement of law, but the
import of McLane Co., Inc. doesn't stop there; the Arkansas
Supreme Court's analysis completely refutes the DFA's assertion
that "the regulation only needs to be reasonable" to be validly
issued.
In McLane Co., Inc., the Arkansas Legislature implemented
a floor on the price of wholesale cigarettes, establishing that it
would be the actual basic cost of the cigarettes plus 2% for the cost
of doing business and ¾% for transportation costs. Id. at 291.
However, the DFA issued a regulation stating instead that the floor
shall be actual basic cost plus 4%. The DFA argued that "because
the DFA interpreted the Act to permit it to promulgate the
Regulation establishing a higher cost, DFA's actions in doing so
should be deemed reasonable." Id. at 299. The Arkansas Supreme
Court strongly disagreed, finding that the DFA's claim that
"reasonableness" controlled failed to address or resolve the second
part of Section 208's limitation which requires that the regulation
not be inconsistent with the law. Id. at 299-300 (stating that the
DFA's reasonableness argument "in no way explains how DFA's
Regulation and its actions fall within the language of the Act."); see
also Weiss v. Maples, 369 Ark. 282, 289 (Ark. 2007) ("[A]ny rule or
regulation adopted by the director of the [DFA] must be consistent
with the law.").
The Arkansas Supreme Court held that the DFA regulation
was contrary to the underlying Act and therefore the regulation was
invalid as a matter of law. Id. at 300. Here, the DFA has admitted
that there is no Arkansas law taxing the Taxpayers with this income,
and further admitted that it was the DFA that adopted Federal law
to tax the Taxpayers with that income. The Arkansas Supreme
48

promulgating regulations which are inconsistent with Arkansas law.
Applied here, the DFA lacks the power to adopt Federal tax law to
tax the Taxpayers.
B. The DFA Cannot “Fill a Void” in Arkansas Law by
Adopting Law of Any Kind.
The DFA further argues that it issued the Regulation because
Section 404 "did not state what interests in a property are sufficient

In Weiss v. McFadden, 356 Ark. 123, 148 S.W.3d 248
(2004), the DFA argued that it could fill a "void" left in the
Arkansas tax code by inserting a section of the Federal tax code. In
that case, the DFA argued that when subsection (c) of Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-307 was invalidated, a "void" existed in the law as to
the treatment of after-tax contributions in employment-related
retirement plans. The DFA argued that it could insert Federal tax
code provision 26 U.S.C. § 72 to fill that void because "'it is logical
to assume the General Assembly would have intended' for Section
72 to be used as a guide." Id. at 132. The Arkansas Supreme Court
firmly disagreed, stating that there was no statutory language
indicating that the Arkansas Legislature intended that Section 72 be
applied to those particular retirement plans, and denied the DFA's
attempt to read Section 72 into Arkansas law, stating, "[w]e will
not read into a statute a provision not put there by the
General Assembly." Id.
After its loss in McFadden, the DFA then promulgated
Emergency Income Tax Rule 2003-4, which again attempted to fill
that same statutory void with Federal tax code Section 72, now
doing so via an Emergency Rule. On appeal, the Arkansas Supreme
Court again firmly held that the DFA could not invoke Section 72 as
law since the Arkansas Legislature had not adopted Section 72 with
regard to those plans. Weiss v. Maples, 369 Ark. 282, 288 (2007).
The Court found that by adopting Section 72 via that Emergency
Rule, that Emergency Rule was "inconsistent" with Arkansas law,
which lacked such a provision. Id. at 289. The Court continued
with a discussion of the separation-of-powers doctrine, and held
that:
[b]ecause an inconsistency existed, the Emergency Rule is
"inconsistent with the law," and "infringe[s] a legislative
function." Accordingly, the Emergency Rule is outside the
49

scope of Weiss's rule-making authority as set forth in § 19-
1-208. Consequently, we also affirm the circuit court's
holding that the Emergency Rule violated the separation-
of-powers doctrine and is, thus, unconstitutional.
Id.
Here, the DFA has attempted to fill a void in Ark. Code Ann.

doesn't matter how the DFA argues or construes it, including by

Arkansas's state government operates under a separation-of-
powers framework, dividing the government into legislative,
executive and judicial departments. Federal Exp. Corp. v. Skelton,
265 Ark. 187, 197 (Ark. 1979). In practice, this means:
The legislative branch of the State government has the
power and responsibility to proclaim the law through
statutory enactments. The judicial branch has the power
and responsibility to interpret the legislative enactments.
The executive branch has the power and responsibility to
enforce the laws as enacted and interpreted by the other
two branches.
Id. at 197- 98; see also Dep't of Human Servs. v. Howard, 367 Ark.
55, 66 (Ark. 2006) (same). These principles dictate that "the
50

functions belonging to one department may not be usurped by the
other, nor may the right to exercise such authority be delegated."
Oates v. Rogers, 144 S.W.2d 457, 458 (Ark. 1940). Though state
executive agencies may possess some legitimate rulemaking
authority, the Arkansas Supreme Court has repeatedly found
executive encroachment into the legislature's domain violates the
separation of powers. See, e.g., Hobbs v. Jones, 412 S.W.3d 844
(Ark. 2012); Patton v. Ragland, 282 Ark. 231 (Ark. 1984); Walden
v. Hart, 420 S.W.2d 868, 870 (Ark. 1967); State ex rel. Atty. Gen. v.
Burnett, 140 S.W.2d 673, 675 (Ark. 1940).
Under the Arkansas Constitution, the taxing power
definitively belongs to the Legislature. Article 5, Section 31 of the
Arkansas constitution provides:
No State tax shall be allowed, or appropriation of money
made, except to raise means for the payment of the just
debts of the State, for defraying the necessary expenses of
government, to sustain common schools, to repel invasion
and suppress insurrection, except by a majority of two-
thirds of both houses of the General Assembly.
Ark. Const. art. V, § 31. Thus, while Ark. Code Ann. § 19-1-208
grants the DFA limited regulatory and rulemaking authority, the
plain enactment of a new tax-i.e., Regulation 4.26-51-102's
adoption of 26 U.S.C. § 671, et seq.-is a power held by the Arkansas
Legislature alone.[Footnote 5 stated that, “The DFA also argues that
the Taxpayers' assertion that Section 675 was invalidly adopted by

of amendment but the power to amend being granted to Congress

The Taxpayers' argument pointed to the fact that when the

Thornbrough, 226 Ark. 768, 294 S.W.2d 62 (1956), and Cheney v.
St. Louis Southwestern Railway Company, 239 Ark. 870, 394
S.W.2d 731 (1965).”]

Ark. Code Ann. § 19-1-208 does not vest the Director with

I. Prior to the Passage of Act 1027 the Director Was
Authorized to Promulgate the Grantor Trust Rules
in Rule 4.26-51-102 of the Comprehensive
Individual Income Tax Regulations.
As has been stated repeatedly throughout this protest, when the
Arkansas General Assembly chose the extraordinarily broad
language for the Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929, it imposed the
tax on " every resident, individual, trust, or estate." Ark. Code
Ann.§ 26-51-201(a) (emphasis added). Then, it defined gross
income broadly to include "[g]ains or profits and income derived
from any source whatever," Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404(a)(1)(E)
(emphasis added), and "[g]ains, profits, and income derived from
dealings in property, whether real or personal, growing out of the
ownership of, use of or interest in the property." Id. at (a)(1)(C)
(emphasis added). This broad language left room for rulemaking
and administrative guidance that is the charge of the Department.
In particular, when the Arkansas General Assembly levied a tax on
gains arising out of an interest in the property, it did not state what
interests in a property render gains on the property as gross income
and subject to the levy. Clearly, not any interest in a property is
sufficient to be subject to tax, so guidance was required for the
Department to carry out its duty to administer the tax.
When the Arkansas General Assembly enacted Act 401 of 1979, it
expressly granted the Director correspondingly broad authority to
promulgate necessary rules for the administration of the Individual
Income Tax. See Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-18-301(a)(1). Out of this
authority, the Director promulgated Rule 4.26-51-102 of the
Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Rules (the "Rule"), which
provides a reasonable answer to the specific question of what
interests in trust property are sufficient to subject gains on the trust
property to the definition of gross income. Previous briefing
elaborates on the process and operation of the grantor trust rules;
that previous explanation is incorporated by reference here.
However, and as stated previously, the grantor trust rules are both
reasonable and do not run contrary to a statute. See McLane Co.,
Inc. v. Weiss, 332 Ark. 284, 965 S.W.2d 109 (1998) ("an agency has
no right to promulgate a rule or regulation contrary to a statute").
Further, they were within the Director's rulemaking authority to
address essential questions that the Arkansas General Assembly has
not to that point answered. That determining the sufficiency of the
interest in a property is an essential question in determining
whether the income tax applies was not seriously challenged in the
hearing or in post-hearing briefs.
64

Further, while the Taxpayers are correct that "when the state seeks
to impose a tax under the terms of a state tax law, then the statute
imposing the tax shall be strictly construed in limitation of the
imposition of the tax," Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313, the Director's
authority to promulgate the grantor trust rules comes from Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-18-301, which does not itself impose a tax. For that
reason, the Director's interpretation of his rulemaking authority
should be highly persuasive and should be upheld unless it is
"clearly wrong." See Macsteel, Parnell Consultants v. Ar. Ok. Gas
C0rp. 363 Ark. 22, 210 S.W.3d 878 (2005). A court will not
attempt to substitute its judgment for that of the administrative
agency. Arkansas Health Services Commission v. Regional Care
Facilities, Inc., 351 Ark. 331, 338, 93 S. W.3d 672 (2002).
Had the Department not promulgated the common-sense grantor
trust rules prior to the passage of Act 1027, there would have been
absurd consequences. For instance, the Department could not have
treated the grantor of a revocable trust as the owner of the trust's
property, which CIITR 7.26-51-102 properly directs as a matter of
common sense. The Arkansas Supreme Court has held that it "does
not engage in interpretations that defy common sense and produce
absurd results." Green v. Mills, 339 Ark. 200, 205, 4 S.W.3d (1999)
(citing Haase v. Starnes, 323 Ark. 262, 915 S . W.2d 675 (1996 )).
Finally, as previously explained, the rule's use of § 675 of the
Internal Revenue Code is not an unconstitutional delegation of
rulemaking power to the United States Congress. First, the
essential and operative parts of the grantor trust rules do not
depend on I.R.C. § 675. The essential parts of the Rule are (1) that a
trust is taxable to the grantor when the grantor retains control over
the income or corpus (trust property) or both to such an extent that
the grantor will be treated as the owner of the property and its
income for income tax purposes and (2) that in determining
whether a trust is a grantor trust, the grantor's degree of control
over the trust must be analyzed. These two statements themselves
do not delegate any authority. Even if the grantor trust rules made
no explicit reference to I.R.C. § 671 et. seq., its analytical framework
on the question of control over trust property would still be relevant
as a matter of common sense. Further, the fact that a portion of a
regulation is void does not invalidate the whole regulation where
such portion is distinctly separable from the remainder which in
itself contains the essentials of a complete regulation. McLane Co.,
Inc. v. Weiss, 332 Ark. 284, 965 S. W.2d 109 (1998). Second, in the
twenty-two years since the grantor trust rules were promulgated,
Congress has not actually amended I.R.C. § 675. Any concern that
65

one might not know what version of I.R.C. § 675 to consult is
unfounded.
The grantor trust rules were duly promulgated within the Director's
broad authority to provide explanation and interpretation required
to meet the duty to enforce the individual income tax, are not
contrary to statute, are reasonable, and do not unconstitutionally
delegate legislative authority. For these reasons, the Director of the
Department of Finance and Administration had the authority prior
to the passage of Act 1027 of 2019 to promulgate Rule 4.26-51-102
of the Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Regulations.

statute [rule] imposing the tax should be strictly construed in
limitation of imposition of the tax and (3) any well-founded doubt
should be resolved against the tax. The General Assembly did not
adopt 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679 until 2019, and only did so
prospectively. The DFA has not and cannot meet its burden to
71

show that the General Assembly adopted 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679 for
tax year 2016. That fact plus the other deficiencies in the DFA's
argument establishes a well-founded doubt under the law.
Pursuant to the requirements of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(1), this
matter must be resolved against the imposition of the DFA's
assessment of tax.
CONCLUSION
Taxpayers respectfully request that the Court find that:
(A) The General Assembly's adoption of 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679
for tax years beginning January 1, 2020 does not permit the DFA to
apply this statute to a tax year ending December 31, 2016;
(B) The DFA failed to meet its burden of proof to establish that
the language in the Rule referencing "See IRC 671, et seq.," would
result in the irrevocable nonresident Trust's gain being
taxed to these Taxpayers for the tax year ending 2016, because 26
U.S.C. §§ 671-679 was not adopted by the General Assembly for any
tax years beginning before January 1, 2020; and
(c) The Department's assessment is void ab initio. [P. 1 – 5].
Despite the numerous arguments raised by the Taxpayers regarding the
invalidity or unconstitutionality of Rule 4.26-51-102, rules promulgated under
the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301(a)(1) (Supp. 2019) are controlling
authority for the Office of Hearings and Appeals. The Office of Hearing and
Appeals is simply not vested with the power to invalidate, overrule, or ignore
rules promulgated under the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301(a)(1)
(Supp. 2019).
With respect to the applicability of Rule 4.26-51-102, the following
testimony and arguments are compelling: (1) the Taxpayers’ Witness stated that
the purpose of the reference “See IRC Sec. 671 et seq.”, in Rule 4.26-51-102, is to
bootstrap those sections up into the regulation; (2) the Tax Auditor stated that he
ultimately used IRC Sec. 675(4)(B) and (C) to determine if the Taxpayers retained
72

a power of administration and should be treated as the owners of the trust; (3)
the Department’s Representative contended that, “[i]n determining whether a
trust is a grantor trust, the Rule states that the grantor's degree of control over
the trust must be analyzed. Id. To aid in this analysis, the Rule utilizes the
circumstances described in IRC § 671 et. seq. to identify when the grantor has
retained such control”;17 and (4) the Taxpayers’ Representative stated that, “[t]he
only manner in which the DFA could possibly tax the Taxpayers on the income
received by the Trust would be through the application of the provisions
of 26 U.S.C. §§ 671 et seq. which is referenced only with the bare word "See" at
the end of Rule 4.26-51-102.”18 The citation to IRC § 671 et seq. and IRC Reg.
1.671-3 provides clear guidance that Rule 4.26-51-102 was intended to be read in
conjunction with the existing federal grantor trust laws and rules.
By applying IRC § 675 through Rule 4.26-51-102, the Department correctly
determined that the Trust was a grantor trust. The Taxpayers’ “power of
administration” (as defined by IRC § 675) satisfied the control requirement of
Rule 4.26-51-102. The income of the Trust was properly imputed to the
Taxpayers pursuant to Rule 4.26-51-102. The arguments raised by the
Taxpayers, regarding the invalidity or unconstitutionality of Rule 4.26-51-102,
are beyond the scope of this administrative review.
Interest was properly assessed upon the tax deficiency for the use of the
State’s tax dollars. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-508 (Supp. 2019).19

The proposed assessment is sustained. The file is to be returned to the

Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-406 (Supp. 2019) provides for the judicial appeal
of a final decision of an Administrative Law Judge or the Commissioner of
