As applicable to the Taxpayer's matter, the analysis under
the statute and regulation is straightforward. First, the
Taxpayer's gross income does include income derived outside the
37

state. Second, the amount of the credit taken as to the tax paid to
was equal to the taxes actually owed by the Taxpayer
to on account of his gambling activity. Third, the
credit did not exceed what the tax would be on the outside income,
if added to the Arkansas income, and calculated at Arkansas
income tax rates. Since the Taxpayer satisfied the statutory
requirements and correctly applied the statutory limitation, the
disallowance by the DFA of Taxpayer's claims for Other State Tax
Credits was improper, and the Taxpayer’s claims for Other State
Tax Credits should be reinstated.
II. THE DFA’S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER STATE
TAX CREDIT IS CONTRARY TO ARK. CODE ANN. §
26-51-504, INCOMPATIBLE WITH THE CURRENT
ARKANSAS INCOME TAX REGIME[Footnote 1
stated, “Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929 (§26-51-
101 et seq.), as amended.], AND CONTRADICTS
OTHER ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE DFA AT
THE ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING.
A. THE DFA’S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER STATE
TAX CREDIT IS CONTRARY TO ARK. CODE ANN. §
26-51-504.
In all but one of the ETAs, Mr. Melson states, "You can not
take a deduction for gambling losses and a tax credit for taxes
paid to other states on the winnings." This statement is wrong
both factually and legally. Factually, the Taxpayer did not take a
tax credit for "taxes paid to other states on the winnings." The
Taxpayer took a tax credit for the taxes he paid to on
account of his gambling activity in . The amount of
taxes owed in took account of the Taxpayers total
income and deductions and calculated his tax obligation
accordingly. This amount, however, was not limited to taxes paid
on his winnings, but rather was a calculation based on income and
deductions on account of his activity in , which is
exactly how Arkansas calculates taxes for its non-residents.
Legally, the limitation on not taking a "deduction for gambling
losses and a tax credit for taxes paid" is not found in Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) or Arkansas Individual Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Therefore, Mr. Melson 's statement
in the ETAs must be rejected.
When applying a tax statute, it must be construed most
strongly against the taxing power. See Ragland v. Quality School
Plan, Inc., 279 Ark. 256, 651 S.W.2d 447 (1983). Furthermore, tax
statutes are to be strictly construed in favor of the taxpayer, and
38

matters not appearing in the statute are not to be read into it. See
Morley v. Pitts, 217 Ark. 755,233 S.W.2d 539 (1950). In Morley,
the taxpayer deducted his losses incurred in drilling dry wells
outside the state of Arkansas. The Commissioner of Revenues for
the State of Arkansas (the ''Commissioner") denied the deductibility
of the expenses, claiming that the Act[Footnote 2 stated that, “As
provided previously, the predecessor to Arkansas Code
Annotated § 26-51-504, was codified from Act 162 of 1943 (the
"Act"). The Act is captioned as: ‘AN ACT to Prevent Double
State Income Taxation of Individual Residents of Arkansas.
Section 1 of the Act provides that when the gross income of an
Arkansas resident includes income derived from property
outside the State or business transacted outside the State, the
Arkansas tax shall be first computed as if all the income were
derived from inside the State; and then a credit shall be given
for the amount of income tax owed by the Arkansas resident to
the State or Territory from which such income has been
received by the taxpayer.’” (Emphasis added)] necessarily
implied that deductions are not to be allowed on losses incurred in
business ventures engaged in outside the State. The taxpayer
challenged the Commissioner's finding, the Chancery Court found
for the taxpayer and the Commissioner appealed. In affirming the
Chancery Court, the Supreme Court noted that the Act does not
mention or attempt to change the statute regarding deductible
items. Instead, "[the Act] is concerned with income and not with
deductions. The purpose of the Act, as stated in the caption, was to
protect an Arkansas resident from double payment of income tax."
Morley, 217 Ark. at 757. The DFA argues that Morley is
inapplicable because the DFA did not deny the deduction for
gambling losses. However, Morley is applicable here because the
DFA is claiming that you cannot take a deduction and a credit
related to the same income (as shown by Mr. Nelson's statement in
his ETAs). This is precisely the issue that Morley held was
inaccurate and that a deduction and credit could be taken
concurrently.
Like its predecessor, Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) is not
concerned with deductions. During his direct examination in the
administrative hearing, Mr. Melson acknowledged that the plain
language of Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-
504(a), which is exclusively relied on by Mr. Melson in the ETAs,
does not contain or support his statement that "You can not take a
deduction for gambling losses and a tax credit for taxes paid to
other states on the winnings." Thus, like the Commissioner in
Morley, Mr. Melson has read into the regulation a limitation that
does not exist: a prohibition of the Other State Tax Credit when a
taxpayer has deductions for gambling losses. Therefore, as was
39

found in Morley, the disallowance of the credit is erroneous
because the limitation imposed by the DFA is not contained in Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 or in Arkansas Individual Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a).
In an attempt to justify his position, Mr. Melson stated during
the administrative hearing that the Taxpayer's sourced
income from his gambling winnings is completely offset by a
deduction for his gambling losses, and, therefore, the Taxpayer did
not pay any additional tax to Arkansas on his gambling winnings.
Authority for this position by Mr. Melson is also not found in Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 or in Arkansas Individual Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Furthermore, as shown below, this
position is inconsistent with Arkansas' current method of
calculating individual income tax.
Neither Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504 nor Arkansas Individual
Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) require netting the items
of out-of-state gross income with the items of out-of-state
deductions to determine the net taxable income and tax owed on
only those out-of-state items. This netting the items of out-of-state
gross income with the items of out-of-state deductions is precisely
the step (hereinafter referred to as the "DFA's Netting Step") that
DFA is now asking this Office to read into Arkansas law. If the
Arkansas General Assembly had intended for this type of
calculation to be made with regard to the Other State Tax Credit,
then it would have provided for this type of calculation in Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-504. Instead, the last sentence of paragraph (a)(1)
reads: "However, credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on
the outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and
calculated at Arkansas income tax rates." The addition of the clause
"if added to the Arkansas income" shows the Arkansas General
Assembly's intent to limit the credit to the total tax liability in
Arkansas, (i.e. on outside income and Arkansas income), so as to
prevent a credit in excess of the tax owed (resulting in a tax refund).
When the DFA interpreted Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504 in
Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a), it clearly agreed with this reading
of the clause and added the following limitation to Arkansas
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a): "Any credit given shall not be allowed
to exceed what the tax would be on all the Arkansas resident's
income, from wherever derived, if such tax was calculated
using Arkansas income tax rates." During the administrative
hearing, Mr. Melson acknowledged that the limitation in the
regulation was intended to prevent a credit in excess of the tax
owed. However, Mr. Melson maintained that the limitation in the
statute was aimed at limiting the credit to the tax owed in Arkansas
40

on the net outside income. The plain language of the statute does
not support this position. Furthermore, Mr. Melson was unable to
offer an explanation at the hearing as to why the limitation in the
statute was not found in the regulation or why the limitation in the
regulation differed from the limitation in the statute. Clearly, Mr.
Melson's feigned ignorance at the hearing was to avoid
acknowledging that the statute and the regulation are consistent
with one another: both limit the credit to the taxpayer's total
Arkansas tax liability and neither limit the credit to the tax owed on
solely the net outside income. Therefore, the DFA's interpretation
of the Other State Tax Credit is contrary to Ark Code Ann. § 26-51-
504 and is improper.
B. THE DFA'S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER
STATE TAX CREDIT IS INCOMPATIBLE WITH
THE CURRENT ARKANSAS INCOME TAX
REGIME.
There is no justification in Arkansas law for netting specific
items of an Arkansas resident taxpayer's individual gross income
with specific items of deductions to determine the net taxable
income and tax owed by the resident as to only those items.
Instead, an Arkansas resident individual taxpayer first calculates
total income by adding together every item of gross income
(without regard to source). See Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-404 and
Form AR1000F, line 21 (a blank AR1000F is attached as Exhibit
A). Then, gross income is adjusted by certain deductions to arrive
at the taxpayer's adjusted gross income. See Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-
51-403 and Form AR1000F, line 23. Then, the taxpayer adds
together every item of deduction (without regard to source) and
nets this amount against adjusted gross income to arrive at net
taxable income. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51- 403 and Form
AR1000F, lines 25 and 26. The tax owed is then calculated by
applying the Arkansas tax table to the net taxable income. See Ark.
Code Ann.§ 26-51-201 and Form AR1000F, line 27.
The amount of the deduction for gambling losses under Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-424 is a function of the amount of gambling
winnings. However, the deductions for gambling losses are
subtracted from gross income (i.e., the income before deductions
are subtracted) along with other deductions to determine the
taxable "net income", which has no identifiable source. Only then,
tax is calculated on the "net income", if any. The drafters of Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 clearly understood that taxable "net
income" does not have identifiable sources. Thus, instead of
requiring taxable "net income" to include income from property or
business outside the state, the statute requires "gross income" to
41

include income from these identifiable "gross income" sources. The
DFA's attempt to calculate tax on specific items of "gross income"
for purposes of the Other State Tax Credit is incompatible with the
current Arkansas income tax regime, which calculates Arkansas
individual resident income tax on "net income" without regard to
source.
C. THE DFA'S APPLICATION OF THE OTHER
STATE TAX CREDIT CONTRADICTS OTHER
ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY THE DFA AT
THE ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING.
During the administrative hearing, Mr. Melson also argued
several times that the Taxpayer paid no tax on his gambling
winnings to Arkansas. He based this claim solely on the fact that
Arkansas allows a deduction for gambling losses to the extent of
gambling winnings and the Taxpayer's losses equaled or exceeded
his winnings in the years at issue. At the hearing, Mr. Melson also
repeatedly stated that the tax paid to was solely on the
gambling winnings because would not have jurisdiction
to tax Arkansas income. Similarly, in the DFA's opening Brief, they
cite Walters v. State of Oklahoma ex rel. Oklahoma and stated that
the "Court determined that the non-Oklahoma income of a non-
resident is used to calculate the Oklahoma income tax rate imposed
on the Oklahoma source income earned by that non-resident, but the
non-Oklahoma income is not taxed." However, Walters v. State of
Oklahoma ex rel. Oklahoma, is a case to determine the
constitutionality of the non-resident income tax system implemented
in Oklahoma. This opinion is not authority that can be relied upon
in Arkansas. Even if it was, the mechanics of the non-resident
income tax calculation were not at issue at that case. The Court's
statement about what was being taxed is dicta based on a statement
provided by the Tax Commission about the general applicability of
the non-resident income tax system and was not the holding of the
case.
However, here, for tax years 2013 through 2017, ,
like Arkansas, allowed a deduction for gambling losses to the extent
of gambling winnings and the Taxpayer still paid taxes to
despite gambling income being the Taxpayer's only taxable activity
that occurred in . When the Taxpayer's representatives
pointed this out, Mr. Melson responded by stating that the reason
the Taxpayer owed tax to on his gambling winnings
despite the deduction for gambling losses (making the gambling
winnings equal $0) was a function of the way that
calculates nonresident income tax. This explanation is
unpersuasive, however, considering that in determining tax liability
42

for non-residents, considers all the Taxpayer's income.
And for some years at issue, the Taxpayer's taxable
income exceed his gambling winnings. See Figure B.
In determining the rate at which nonresidents' income is
taxed, most states consider only the income that is taxable by the
state. A growing number of states, however, including
and Arkansas, determine nonresidents' tax liability by reference to
the nonresidents' total income, wherever earned. Thus, both
and Arkansas considered all of the Taxpayer's income,
from wherever earned, in arriving at the tax owed to each respective
state for the years at issue. Similarly, for 2013 through 2017, both
states allowed a deduction for gambling losses to the extent of
gambling winnings. The DFA offered no explanation as to how the
taxes paid to were solely on the gambling winnings, yet
no taxes paid to Arkansas are attributable to gambling winnings,
when both states offered the same offsetting deduction for
gambling losses. Since the DFA offered no explanation for these
contradictory positions advanced by the DFA at the hearing and in
its opening brief, these positions cannot be relied on to disallow the
Other State Tax Credit.
III. THE TAXPAYER WOULD BE SUBJECTED TO
DOUBLE TAXATION IF THE DISALLOWANCE OF THE
OTHER STATE TAX CREDIT IS NOT REINSTATED.
Although "double taxation" is not mentioned in the language
of Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504, the legislative intent behind the
Act[Footnote 3 stated, “See note 2.”], the predecessor to Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-504, was clearly to prevent double taxation of
Arkansas residents. Arkansas Individual Income Tax Regulation §
1.26-51-504(a) contains an additional requirement not found in the
statute: "No credit shall be allowed against the resident's Arkansas
income tax liability unless the resident can clearly show that he or
she would be subject to double taxation on a portion of his or
her income unless the credit is allowed." It is worth noting that a
plain reading of the language of this requirement does not demand
the Taxpayer show double taxation of any specific source, amount
or type of income. Instead, this additional limitation only requires
the Taxpayer to show "a portion of his or her income," not a portion
of his or her source income, is subject to double taxation in order
for the credit to be allowed. This was confirmed by Mr. Melson
during the administrative hearing. Furthermore, this additional
limitation does not change the amount of the credit that is
otherwise allowed. Thus, if a taxpayer is able to show a portion of
his or her income is subject to double taxation, the credit would be
equal to the lesser of taxes actually owed to such other state(s) or the
43

total tax liability in Arkansas. Since the Taxpayer can clearly show a
portion of his income is subject to double taxation, the full amount of
the credits claimed on the Taxpayer's Forms AR1000F (equal to the
amounts in the fourth column of Figure B, above) must be
reinstated.
Arkansas and each take into consideration the
Taxpayer's total income from all sources in determining the taxes
owed to the state. In this way, the Taxpayer's total income is
subject to tax in each state in which they earned income. In order
to ensure taxpayers are not subject to double taxation,
applies a percentage to the net taxable income of nonresidents
reflecting the percentage of total income earned in the state. (Note:
Arkansas applies this same method for determining taxes owed by
nonresidents to Arkansas). However, no limiting percentage is
applied to the income of Arkansas residents who earn income and
pay taxes to other states (i.e., Arkansas taxes its residents on 100%
of their income wherever derived). Instead, Arkansas residents are
entitled to the Other State Tax Credit to ensure they are not subject
to double taxation on any portion of their income.
In this matter, double taxation is demonstrated in the
following table. The second column represents the Taxpayer's total
state income tax liability if his gambling activities partially occurred
in and the credit is disallowed in Arkansas. The third
column represents the Taxpayer’s total state income tax liability if
his gambling activities only occurred in Arkansas. The fourth
column is the difference.
Year
This table shows that the Taxpayer is paying $ more
in state income taxes on the exact same amount of total
income simply because the Taxpayer chose to gamble in
. Keep in mind that, except in 2018, both Arkansas and
allowed the Taxpayer a deduction for gambling losses
that fully offset his gambling winnings (such that, under the DFA's
analysis, his net taxable gambling winnings in both states are $0).
Thus, this $ difference cannot be explained by a difference
44

in the states' taxing methods relating to gambling. Furthermore, in
each year at issue, income tax rates are lower than
Arkansas' income tax rates. Thus, this $ difference cannot
be explained away by a difference in the states' tax rates. The only
plausible explanation is that both states are taxing some portion of
the same income. This fact, which was admitted by Mr. Melson
during the administrative hearing, conclusively demonstrates that the
Taxpayer is subject to double taxation unless the Other State Tax
Credit is allowed.
IV. THE DFA'S RELIANCE ON LAWS FROM OTHER
STATES IS UNPERSUASIVE AND SHOULD BE
DISREGARDED.
As previously stated, the only question to be decided in this
matter is whether the Taxpayer's application of the Other State Tax
Credit was justified under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504. This
question hinges on the interpretation of the following language:
"However, the credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on the
outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and calculated at
Arkansas income tax rates." The introduction to the Arkansas
Individual Income Tax Regulations (Regulation 1997-4) states:
Pursuant to the authority vested in the Commissioner of
Revenues and in compliance with Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
301 and § 26-51-104, the Commissioner of Revenues of the
Department of Finance and Administration, with the
approval of the Governor, does hereby promulgate the
following rules and regulations for the enforcement and
administration of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51- 101 et seq.
PURPOSE OF THE REGULATIONS: The following
regulations are promulgated to implement and clarify the
Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929 (§ 26-51-101 et seq.), as
amended. All persons affected by or relying upon these
regulations are advised to read them in their entirety, as the
meaning of the provisions of one regulation may depend
upon the provisions contained in another regulation.
Thus, the DFA promulgated Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-
504(a) for the exact purpose of clarifying Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a).
Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) is the only authority cited
authority in the ETAs for disallowing the Other State Tax Credit, yet
it is not cited or relied on at all by the DFA in its opening brief.
Perhaps this glaring omission reveals that the DFA has taken a
45

position contrary to Income Tax Regulation§ 1.26-51-504(a).
Regardless, pursuant to the plain language of the regulation, the
credit is limited to the Taxpayer's total Arkansas tax liability,
regardless of source. The DFA, by avoiding the language of the
regulation, is attempting to ignore its own regulation that interprets
the statute in question, and, instead, is attempting to adopt a new
interpretation that would limit the credit to the taxes paid to
Arkansas solely on the other state source income. This new
interpretation is based on the DFA's newly invented method of
calculation that includes the DFA's Netting Step that is first
mentioned in Paragraph II.A above.
However, the DFA fails to cite a single source of precedential
authority to support its new interpretation of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-
51-504(a) and the resulting method of calculation. Instead, the
DFA cites a tax treatise analyzing the laws of states other than
Arkansas and cases from Oklahoma and New Jersey. This
nonbinding authority does not override the DFA's own
interpretation from Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) and
such authority is not binding on this Office. Furthermore, the DFA's
reliance on case law from other jurisdictions and secondary sources
analyzing the laws of other states is unpersuasive as the DFA failed
to argue why such authority should apply to the instant case instead
of applying the applicable regulation that the DFA promulgated.
Obviously, the DFA does not like the results provided by the current
Arkansas laws applicable here.
Mere citation of another jurisdiction's authority is not
singularly persuasive to prove that the State of Arkansas should
interpret a case similarly. Brown v. Arkansas Dep't of Correction,
339 Ark. 458 (1999) (citing Rockefeller v. Rockefeller, 980 S.W.2d
255 (1998)). The sheer numbers of decisions of other jurisdictions
one way or the other on any given question are not controlling on
Arkansas courts. Chamberlin v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.,
343 Ark. 392, at 398 (2001) (quoting Clampit v. State Farm Mut.
Auto. Ins. Co., 828 S.W.2d 593 (1992)).
In Chamberlin, the Arkansas Supreme Court stated:
Appellant's reliance on authority from other jurisdictions
is equally unpersuasive. Not only is the cited case law not
controlling on this court but, in many cases, it is clearly
distinguishable. Other states' decisions turned upon
specific language in the state's statute authorizing
stacking or an expressed legislative intent favoring
stacking.
46

Chamberlin, 343 Ark. at 398. Like the authority cited by the
appellant in Chamberlin, the authority cited by the DFA is clearly
distinguishable. The treatise and the case law cited by the DFA
each analyze the specific statutory and regulatory language from
other states that have implemented their own version of the other
state tax credit. Since the specific language found in these states'
statutes differs from the language of the Arkansas statute, the
interpretation of the language of such other state statutes by a
foreign court or by a secondary source cannot lend itself to the
interpretation of an Arkansas statute with completely different
language.
For example, in its opening brief, the DFA cites heavily to
¶20.10 of the third edition of the state tax treatise entitled "State
Taxation" by Jerome R. Hellerstein and Walter Hellerstein. See
Hellerstein & Hellerstein, State Taxation, ¶ 20.10, at 20-81 (3rd ed.
2003). This tax treatise summarizes and analyzes state statutory,
regulatory and case law related to state taxation, and ¶20.10
discussed state laws relating to credits for taxes paid to other states.
Unfortunately for the DFA, the authors do not summarize, analyze,

tax liability is a function of the income tax imposed by
and is not attributable to any double taxation by Arkansas.
Accordingly, Taxpayer was not double taxed by Arkansas and the
other state tax credit claimed by Taxpayer was properly denied by
DFA.
6. Decisions From Other States are Instructive
DFA disagrees with Taxpayer's contention that cases cited by
DFA from other jurisdictions are not relevant. In the absence of
Arkansas case law interpreting the other state tax credit limitation
60

in Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1), decisions of appellate courts
regarding similar cases are instructive.
DFA agrees that state laws differ, and the way states calculate
their other state tax credit vary. However, the principles espoused
in those cases are relevant. For example, in the case of Stiber v.
Director, Division of Taxation, 9 NJ Tax 623 (1988) the relevant
principle is that an interpretation of the other state tax credit to
allow a credit based on income not taxed in the state allowing the
credit is an absurd result. As the Court stated in that case:
To include in the maximum credit factor the foreign income
which was not taxed by New Jersey would be at variance
with the provisions of section (a) and would reach the
absurd result of having New Jersey grant a credit against its
tax on New Jersey income on the basis that a resident
taxpayer had paid a tax to a foreign jurisdiction on income
which was not taxable in New Jersey.
Taxpayer proposes an interpretation of the limitation in Ark.
Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) that leads to just such an absurd result.
On page 2 of Taxpayer's brief he says "After fully offsetting the
gambling winnings by the gambling losses (i.e., gambling winnings
subject to tax were $0) . . . " Taxpayer clearly recognizes that he paid
no Arkansas income tax on his gambling winnings. Yet Taxpayer
contends that the Arkansas General Assembly enacted the other
state tax credit with the intention that it be interpreted to offset the
Arkansas income tax he owes on his Arkansas source income. He
makes this argument ignoring that the stated legislative intent for
the credit, as expressed in Act 162 of 1943, was to prevent double
taxation and that no part of his source income was
double taxed by Arkansas.
It is well established that a statute should not be interpreted in
a way that reaches an absurd result. Curry v. Pope County
Equalization Bd., 2011 Ark. 408, at 10-11, 385 S.W.3d 130, 136.
Additionally, Taxpayer's interpretation is contrary to the rules of
construction set out above in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313.
Accordingly, Taxpayer's interpretation of the credit limitation in
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) must be rejected.
7. The Treatment of Nonresident Taxpayer Under
Arkansas Law is a Matter of Policy Within the Purview of
the Arkansas General Assembly and is not Relevant to
This Matter.
Taxpayer compares the treatment of residents and
nonresidents by the state of Arkansas to demonstrate inconsistent
61

treatment. The Arkansas General Assembly enacted the taxation
method applicable to nonresidents on their income from Arkansas
sources. That methodology is outlined in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
435. The General Assembly also enacted the limitation on the
credit for taxes paid to other states in Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-
504(a)(1). The Arkansas Supreme Court has explained that the
Arkansas General Assembly is the sole arbiter of policy decisions
within Arkansas and it would be inappropriate for an
administrative agency or court to refuse to enforce a state law as it
reads based on a policy disagreement. See Snowden v. JRE
Investments, Inc., 2010 Ark. 276, 370 S.W.3d 215. Until amended,
these statutory provisions are controlling. If Taxpayer has a
disagreement with the policy outlined in either of those provisions,
it is the General Assembly's duty to address policy issues. Until that
time, the treatment of nonresident taxpayers under Arkansas law is
not relevant to the case at hand.
CONCLUSION
State law must be applied as it reads and to give effect to the
legislative intent in its enactment. Act 162 of 1943 expressed that
the purpose of the credit for tax paid to another state, as codified at
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1), is to prevent double taxation.
Under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313, Taxpayer has the burden of
proving his entitlement to the other state tax credit. When the rules
of construction outlined in the Arkansas Code are applied here, the
facts and law reveal that Taxpayer has failed to prove entitlement to
the other state tax credit because he paid no Arkansas income tax
on his source income. Taxpayer's efforts to claim that
credit as an offset against his Arkansas source income exceeds the
limitation outlined in the last sentence of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a)(1), violates the legislative purpose in its enactment and must
be denied. [P. 1 – 16].
Taxpayer’s Reply Brief to Response Brief of DFA
The issue to be decided in this matter is the correct
interpretation of the following language from Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-
51-504(a)(1): "However, credit shall not exceed what the tax would
be on the outside income, if added to the Arkansas income, and
calculated at Arkansas income tax rates." This is the issue because
this is the language from the statute on which the DFA is relying to
deny the Taxpayer's other state tax credit that is allowed by Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504 ("Other State Tax Credit"). Much to the
chagrin of the DFA "tax acts are to be construed in favor of the
taxpayer; and matters not appearing in a taxing Statute are not to
62

be read into it when such result is adverse to the taxpayer through
implication." Morely v. Pitts, 217 Ark. 755, 757 (1950).
Furthermore, the doctrine of strict construction is to use the plain
meaning of the statutory language employed. Lawhon Farm
Services v. Brown, 335 Ark. 272, 279 (1996).
The Taxpayer's interpretation of the above quoted statutory
language is the exact same as the DFA's interpretation at the time it
promulgated Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a), which is that
this language limits the credit to the total tax paid to Arkansas on
income from all sources, wherever derived. The DFA's
interpretation as of 2019 is that this language requires a series of
calculations involving calculating tax on all sources, then
recalculating tax by excluding income from outside sources, then
netting the two results. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) is not
ambiguous, and a strict construction of its language simply does not
support the DFA's revised interpretation.
In its brief, the DFA states that the language "[h]owever,
credit shall not exceed what the tax would be on the outside income,
if added to the Arkansas income, and calculated at Arkansas income
tax rates" from Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) limits the amount
of the credit and requires a calculation to be made. The Taxpayer
agrees. The above quoted language from the statute can be easily
converted to a mathematical formula. If "outside income" equals
"OI", "Arkansas income" equals "AI", and "Arkansas income tax
rates" equals "TR", then the calculation called for by a plain reading
of the language from Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) is as follows:
Credit Limitation = (OI + AI)TR.
The Taxpayer's formula is straightforward and it is easy to see its
justification from a plain reading of Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-
504(a)(1). However, if we were to use the DFA's interpretation, the
calculation called for is as follows:
Credit Limitation= (OI+ AI)TR - (AI)TR
Support for the DFA's formula is not contained in a plain reading of
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) and would instead require
substantial new language to be inserted into the statute in order to
achieve the DFA's desired result.
The DFA has again cited to a non-Arkansas case interpreting
a non-Arkansas statute, specifically a statute with a different
formula and a case analyzing a different issue. The DFA relies on
Stearns v. Arizona Department of Revenue as support for its
63

proposition that Taxpayer must determine the Arkansas tax due
solely on Taxpayer's source income (i.e., the gambling
winnings) in determining the amount of the credit allowed to
Taxpayer. In Stearns v. Arizona Department of Revenue, the
Arizona Court was tasked with determining the limitation placed on
a resident's use of a credit for taxes paid in other states. See 231 Ariz.
172, 173 (2012). However, the sole issue decided in Stearns was
whether Arizona's credit calculation required using a taxpayer's
gross income (income before deductions and exemptions) or
taxpayer's taxable income (income after deductions and exemptions).
The definition of income subject to tax is not the issue that is in
question here. As discussed below, out of state case law, and even in-
state case law is not necessary to interpret what has already been
interpreted by the DFA's own regulation. But even if one were to
consider this out of state case, Stearns does not support the DFA's
interpretation of Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) that you must net
the source income with the source deductions
in order to determine the Arkansas allowable credit.
The DFA goes on for several pages of its Brief about
graduated income tax rates. This discussion is irrelevant to the
issue here and is ostensibly included in an attempt to intentionally
make this issue seem more complicated than it is. To this end, the
DFA would have the Administrative Law Judge believe that Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) limits the credit to the taxes paid on
just the outside income, and the phrase "if added to the Arkansas
income" was included to ensure that the tax on the outside income is
calculated at the highest marginal rate. As to this argument, the
DFA's attempt to justify its desired result fails for the following
reasons.
First, as argued above, in order to calculate the tax on just the
outside income at the highest marginal tax rate a series of
interrelated calculations must be performed. As shown above, a
series of interrelated calculations is clearly not called for by the
language of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) and Income Tax
Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Second, the DFA fails to explain why
Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) includes the following
limitation: "Any credit given shall not be allowed to exceed what the
tax would be on all the Arkansas resident's income, from wherever
derived, if such tax was calculated using Arkansas income tax rates."
At the hearing, the DFA argued that the regulation contains two
limitations: one equal to the tax on income from all sources, and a
second one equal to the tax on just the outside income. However, if
the statute contained a limitation equal to the tax on just the outside
income, a second limitation equal to the tax on income from all
sources would be superfluous. The tax on just the outside income
64

could never be greater than the tax on income from all sources.
Thus, this second limitation would be completely unnecessary,
making its inclusion in the regulation illogical and against basic
rules of statutory interpretation. "The rule against superfluities
instructs courts to interpret a statute to effectuate all its provisions,
so that no part is rendered superfluous." Hibbs v. Winn, 542 U.S.
88, 89 (2004).
As demonstrated by the Taxpayer in his first brief, the
language in the regulation tracks the language of Ark. Code Ann. §
26-51-504(a)(1) such that it is easy to tell which sentence of the
statute each sentence of the regulation is interpreting. The DFA
would have the Administrative Law Judge believe that the limitation
in the regulation equal to the tax on income from all sources is not
interpreting the language from the statute at issue in this matter.
However, there is no other possible language that the sentence of
limitation in the regulation could be interpreting. The DFA knows
this to be true, but would have the Administrative Law Judge ignore
the limitation from the regulation since it results in an
interpretation of the statute that does not support the DFA's desired
interpretation of Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1).
Instead, the DFA argues that the following language from the
regulation interprets the language from the statute at issue in this
matter: "No credit shall be allowed against the resident's Arkansas
income tax liability unless the resident can clearly show that he or
she would be subject to double taxation on a portion of his or her
income unless the credit is allowed." This language clearly places an
additional burden of proof requirement on the Taxpayer. However,
it clearly does not call for a specific calculation of an additional
limitation. Furthermore, as argued by the Taxpayer in his original
brief, this additional burden of proof does not require the Taxpayer
to show double taxation of any specific source, amount or type of
income. Instead, it only requires the Taxpayer to show "a portion
of his or her income" would be subject to double taxation to be entitled
to the credit as otherwise limited to the tax on income from all sources.
The Taxpayer previously met this burden of proof by showing his
total tax liability on the exact same amount of total income would
be $ greater if the credit is denied even though (1) both
Arkansas and allowed a deduction for gambling losses
equal to gambling winnings and (2) income tax rates are
lower than Arkansas' income tax rates.
As just stated, in all years in question gambling winnings
were the only source income of Taxpayer and these were
fully offset by gambling losses for both Arkansas and
income tax purposes (other than 2018 due to an law change
65

that limited the gambling loss deduction). Despite these facts, the
following chart shows the Arkansas taxable income (the income to
which the Arkansas income tax rates are applied after all allowable
deductions are subtracted - including gambling losses) and the
taxable income (the income to which the
income tax rates are applied after all allowable deductions are
subtracted - including gambling losses) to further show the
"portion" of Taxpayer's income that is being subjected to double
taxation:
Year
This is the portion of the income that both Arkansas and
are actually subjecting to tax and clearly shows that
double taxation is occurring. On page 6 of the DFA's Brief, the DFA
states a ''taxpayer is not entitled to the other state tax credit unless
a portion of his income is being taxed by both Arkansas and another
state." The Taxpayer agrees with this statement and the above table
shows the portion of the Taxpayer's income that is being taxed by
both Arkansas and
The DFA also would have the Administrative Law Judge
interpret an Arkansas statute using case law from other states. Case
law from other states is completely irrelevant and unpersuasive
because those cases are interpreting different statutes and different
credit limitations. Furthermore, here, case law is not necessary due
to the fact that the DFA already provided such an interpretation by
promulgating Income Tax Regulation§ 1.26-51-504(a). It is not
until recently that the DFA has decided it doesn't like its own
interpretation and has thus turned to out of state cases to attempt
to justify its incorrect application of the out of state tax credit.
However, since the DFA's own regulation provides a perfectly clear
interpretation, there is no need to consider case law at all. The
DFA's desire to avoid its own original interpretation in favor of a
new, more favorable interpretation is not grounds for considering
out of state cases. Since the Taxpayer's interpretation of Ark. Code
Ann.§ 26-51-504(a)(1) is the same as the DFA's interpretation in
Income Tax Regulation§ 1.26-51-504(a), the DFA's new
interpretation must be rejected.
66

To achieve the DFA's desired result in Arkansas, there are
states with other state tax credit statutes that do expressly call for
such a calculation. Ostensibly, this is why the DFA has repeatedly
cited to out of state non-binding authorities. However, Arkansas is
not one of them and it would be unfair to read them into Arkansas
law ex post facto. Due to the fact that Arkansas law does not set
forth the steps the DFA desires, a plain reading of Ark. Code Ann. §
26-51-504(a)(1) and Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a) does
not provide for the calculation the DFA seeks to impose. For this
reason, the DFA should go through the legislative process to get the
General Assembly to change Arkansas law in order to obtain the
DFA's desired result, but adding language to a statute is not
something that should be done in this proceeding.
Finally, in its response brief, the DFA states that it would be
"inappropriate for an administrative agency or court to refuse to
enforce a state law as it reads based on a policy disagreement." The
Taxpayer could not agree more. The Taxpayer's interpretation of
the language from Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) at issue here is
supported by Income Tax Regulation § 1.26- 51-504(a). This
interpretation, as it currently reads, entitles the Taxpayer to the
Other State Tax Credit. Until amended to include the additional
steps and limitations desired by the DFA, the DFA will have to
accept the Other State Tax Credit as written, regardless of how
"absurd" it believes the results.
CONCLUSION
Based on the foregoing, the Taxpayer asks that the
Administrative Law Judge reverse the DFA's disallowance of the
Other State Tax Credit so that Taxpayer is not subjected to double
taxation on his income causing him to pay an additional $
in tax liability that was intended by the Arkansas General Assembly
to be avoided through the use of the Other State Tax Credit. [P. 1 –
7].
Individual Income Tax Assessments and Adjustments
The State of Arkansas imposes an income tax upon “the entire income of
every resident, individual, trust, or estate. The tax shall be levied, collected, and
paid annually upon the entire net income as defined and computed in this
chapter at the following rates . . ..” See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201(a) (Supp.
2017). “Gross income” includes “[g]ains, profits, and income derived from any
67

source whatever[.]” See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404(a)(1)(E) (Supp. 2017). “Net
income” is derived from adjusting gross income by any allowed deductions. See
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-403 (Repl. 2012).
Tax deductions and credits, like tax exemptions, exist as a matter of
legislative grace. See Cook, Commissioner of Revenue v. Walters Dry Good
Company, 212 Ark. 485, 206 S.W.2d 742 (1947); and Kansas City Southern Ry.
Co. v. Pledger, 301 Ark. 564, 785 S.W.2d 462 (1990). A taxpayer claiming a
deduction or credit bears the burden of proving that it is entitled to the deduction
or credit by bringing herself or himself clearly within the terms and conditions
imposed by the statute that contains the deduction or credit. See Weiss v.
American Honda Finance Corp., 360 Ark. 208, 200 S.W.3d 381 (2004).
Initially, it must be determined if the Arkansas Supreme Court has issued
an opinion interpreting the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) which
would be controlling precedent given the facts of this case. The Taxpayer’s
reliance on the holding in Morley v. Pitts, supra, is misplaced (See Brief of
Taxpayer – P. 8 – 10). The Office of Hearings and Appeals has previously issued
decisions which determined that holding in Morley v. Pitts, supra, is not
controlling authority in cases involving the proper calculation of other state tax
credit.
Ultimately, the resolution of this case depends on a determination of
whether the Department correctly adjusted the Taxpayer’s income tax returns for
the relevant tax years. The Department’s adjustments of the Taxpayer’s income
tax returns were based upon its interpretation of the provisions of Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-51-504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012). The interpretation of statutes by an
68

administrative agency, while not conclusive, is highly persuasive. Aluminum Co.
of America v. Weiss, 329 Ark. 225, 946 S.W.2d 695 (1997). An administrative
agency’s interpretation of a statute or its own rules will not be overruled unless it
is clearly wrong. Arkansas Dep’t. of Human Servs. v. Hillsboro Manor Nursing,
304 Ark. 476, 803 S.W.2d 891 (1991). The Arkansas Supreme Court has
recognized that administrative agencies are often required to interpret statutes
and rules. Walnut Grove School Distr. No. 6 of Boone County v. County Board of
Education, 204 Ark. 354, 162 S.W.2d 64 (1942).
In McCourt Mfg. Corp. v. Rycroft, 2009 Ark. 332, 322 S.W. 3d 491, the
Arkansas Supreme Court discussed a rule of statutory construction which
provides that courts should strive to reconcile statutory provisions relating to the
same subject to make them sensible, consistent, and harmonious. Applying that
rule of statutory construction to the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012), it is obvious that the second sentence of the subdivision
operates to limit the credit provided in the first sentence of the subdivision.
Accordingly, after consideration of the extensive arguments and citations
contained in the post-hearing briefs and the evidence presented by the parties, a
preponderance of the evidence supports a finding that the Department’s
interpretation of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012) (“If the Arkansas
income tax due on the outside income, when added to the Arkansas income, is $0
there is no credit available for taxes paid on that income to another state.” See
Department’s Response to Brief of Taxpayer – P. 10) is not clearly wrong.
The Department has statutory authority to “[a]udit and properly
determine and compute the state tax payable by any taxpayer subject to taxation
69

under any state law”16 and to “employ proper and reasonable audit methods.”17
The greater weight of evidence in the record supports a finding that the audit
methods employed by the Tax Auditor were reasonable and that the Taxpayer
was not subjected to double taxation on his income within Arkansas.18
While the Taxpayer demonstrated that the earning of the income within
resulted in an increased total tax liability for the Taxpayer (when all
state taxes are added), the Taxpayer has not clearly shown that the increase in
total tax was the due to double taxation as opposed to differing state tax policies.
See Income Tax Regulation § 1.26-51-504(a). Consequently, the Department
correctly assessed tax against the Taxpayer (and properly denied the refund
claim) for the years in the audit period.19
Interest was properly assessed upon the tax deficiencies for the use of the
State’s tax dollars. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-508 (Repl. 2012). No penalty was
assessed against the Taxpayer.
DECISION AND ORDER
The proposed assessments and refund claim denial are sustained. The file
is to be returned to the appropriate section of the Department for further
proceedings in accordance with this Administrative Decision and applicable law.
16 See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301(a)(2) (Repl. 2012).
17 See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-305(a)(2)(A) (Repl. 2012).
18 The Taxpayer’s gambling winnings were entirely offset by the deduction of gambling losses.
Persuasive authority from other jurisdictions support the Department’s position in this matter.
See Walters v. State of Oklahoma ex rel. Oklahoma Tax Commission, 935 P. 2d 398 (1996) and
Stiber v. Director, Division of Taxation, 9 NJ Tax 623 (1988).
19 To the extent the Taxpayer is challenging the constitutionality of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
504(a)(1) (Repl. 2012), the statute is presumed to be constitutional. See Parkman v. Sex Offender
Screening and Risk Assessment Committee, 2009 Ark. 205 at 1 (2009). Furthermore, the Office
of Hearings and Appeals does not have jurisdiction or authority to determine the constitutionality
of a statute. See Arkansas Tobacco Control Bd. v. Sitton, 357 Ark. 357, 166 S.W.3d 550 (2004).
None of the remaining arguments set forth in the Taxpayer’s post-hearing briefs, concerning the
Department’s purported erroneous application of the law, are persuasive.
70

title: Arkansas DFA Administrative Decision No. 23-226,23-227,23-228
text:
Attorneys at Law, Revenue Legal Counsel. The Taxpayer was represented by
. The Department's Opening
Brief was filed November 4, 2022. The Taxpayer’s Response Brief was filed on
December 5, 2022. The Department's Reply Brief was filed on December 19,
2022. The matter was submitted for a decision on February 10, 2023.
ISSUE
Whether the assessments of sales and special excise taxes, issued by the
Department against the Taxpayer, should be sustained?4 Subject to the agreed
upon adjustments, yes in part.
FINDINGS OF FACT/CONTENTIONS OF THE PARTIES
The Department’s Opening Brief set forth its position in this case and
stated, in pertinent part, as follows:
The Office of Revenue Legal Counsel submits the following letter
brief. The legal issues in this case are: (1) whether the Taxpayer
owes sales tax on sales of event venue rental packages that include
the rental of the venue and tangible personal property; (2) whether
the Taxpayer owes compensating use tax on out of state purchases
of tangible personal property; and (3) whether the Taxpayer owes
short term rental tax on its sales of event venue rental packages.
BACKGROUND
("Taxpayer") is a
owned by . Taxpayer is a
The
rental amount for the property includes the use of tables, chairs and
linens for those events. On June 17, 2021, an auditor for the
Department, Wade Gambill ("Auditor"), sent an Audit Appointment
Letter requesting records for the periods of June 01, 2018 through
May 31, 2021, including tax reports and return, tax accruals,
purchase invoices, sales invoices, bank statements, credit card
statements, check registers, journals and ledgers, and other records.
4 See Footnote 2.
2

Because Taxpayer was a non-filer, the audit period was extended to
cover June 1, 2018 to December 31, 2021.
During the audit, the Taxpayer provided some, but not all, contracts
during the audit period because the Taxpayer did not keep their
contracts or invoices based on the belief that their sales were not
taxable. Additionally, the auditor reviewed bank statements and
tax returns for the audit period. After a review of the Taxpayer's
contracts, the Auditor determined that the rental of the property
included the taxable sale of tangible personal property, including
tables, chairs, and linens. Accordingly, because the Taxpayer did
not provide itemized invoices for each rental, the Auditor
determined that each rental sale was a taxable transaction.
The auditor further determined that the Taxpayer had not collected
or remitted sales taxes for any of the rentals for state, city, tourism
or short-term rental. The gross receipts from the bank records and
other records provided by the Taxpayer were used to assess the
taxes owed. The rentals for the
were assessed for state, county and short-term rental since the price
for the rental of the venue included use of tangible personal
property and a cleaning service after each event. Without separate
itemized invoices or contracts, the only way the audit could be
conducted was on the gross receipts for each event and for gross
receipts for the use of the rental property. Accordingly, the Auditor
determined that each bank deposit was a taxable sale transaction.
. . .
The auditor prepared schedules of his findings. As a result of the
audit, the Department assessed the Taxpayer gross receipts taxes
(sales taxes), compensating use taxes (use taxes) and special excise
taxes. On July 11, 2022, the Department issued a Summary of
Findings based on the audit, which assessed a total of
The assessment for sales tax was in the amount of
including in tax, in penalty, and
in interest. . . . The assessment also consisted of a special excise
short term rental tax in the amount of , including
in tax, in penalty, and in interest.
On July 14, 2022, the Department issued a Notice of Proposed
Assessment based upon the accounting audit using records
provided by the Taxpayer or secured by the auditor and examined
during the audit.
3

The Taxpayer filed this protest on September 9, 2022. Taxpayer's
representative expressed that Taxpayer wished to protest the
assessment, but did not advance arguments against the assessment.
. . .
The Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax (commonly referred to as "sales
tax") generally applies to all sales of tangible personal property
unless a specific statutory exemption is applicable. Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-52-301 (Repl. 2021). A "sale" means the transfer of either the
title or possession of tangible personal property including as a lease
or rental of that tangible personal property. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-
52-103(20), (31) (Repl. 2021). Thus, during the events held on the
property, the Taxpayer provides for the use of tables, chairs and
linens, and the contract is treated as a sale for tax purposes. See
Exhibit 1. On page 5 of the contract found in Exhibit 1 states that
the venue includes with every rental:
Taxpayer cannot argue that the use of tables, chairs, linens, and
other tangible personal property are complimentary when they are
included in "every rental" of the venue. Therefore, these items are
included in the total rental price for the property.
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-103(2)(A) defines a bundled transaction as
a retail sale of two or more products, except real property and
services to real property, in which the products are otherwise
distinct and identifiable and are sold for one nonitemized price.
The statute also states that a bundled transaction does not include
the sale of any product in which the sales price varies or is
negotiable based on the selection by the purchaser of the
products included in the transaction. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-
52-103(2)(B). Thus, these transactions are not "bundled
transactions" as defined by the Arkansas law.
In Weiss v. Best Enterprises, Inc., 323 Ark. 712, 917 S.W.2d 543
(1996), the Court held that where the contract or bill for the rental
of items and/or services must be clear and itemized or the whole
transaction is taxable. In Leathers v. A & B Dirt Movers, Inc., 311
Ark. 320, 844 S.W.2d 314 (1992), the Court held that even though
the taxpayer asserted that he was " hauling free dirt " and thus the
4

transaction was not taxable, the transaction was for hauling dirt
and without records that separate the taxable from the non-taxable

Generally, the liability for collection and remittance of sales tax is
upon the seller of the tangible personal property. See Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-52-508(a) (Repl. 2020). A seller, however, may be
relieved of this liability if the purchaser makes an exemption claim
and the seller obtains identifying information of the purchaser and
the reason the purchaser is claiming the exemption in the manner
prescribed by the Department. See Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax
Rule GR-79(C); see also Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-517 (Repl. 2020).
. . .
The liability for the payment of taxes imposed under any state tax
law is on the taxpayer. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-501 (Repl. 2020). It
is the duty of taxpayers to maintain adequate records reflecting
their business activities, taxable transactions, and the accuracy of
their reported and paid taxes. The Arkansas Tax Procedure Act at
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-506 (Repl. 2020) specifically provides as
follows regarding this issue:
(a) It is the duty of every taxpayer required to
make a return of any tax due under any state tax law to
keep and preserve suitable records as are necessary to
determine the amount of tax due or to prove the accuracy of
any return.
(b) Unless otherwise provided by law, the taxpayer is
required to keep and maintain all records within the State
of Arkansas and for at least six (6) years after a return was
filed. These records are subject to examination by the
director at any reasonable time.
. . . .
(d) When a taxpayer fails to preserve and maintain
the records required by any state tax law, the director may,
in his or her discretion, make an estimated assessment
based upon information available to him or her as
to the amount of tax due by the taxpayer. The burden of
proof of refuting this estimated assessment is upon the
taxpayer. [Emphasis added].
5

See also Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax Rule GR-80(C).
In Leathers v. A & B Dirt Movers, Inc., 311 Ark. 320, 325, 844
S.W.2d 314, 317 (1992), the Arkansas Supreme Court stated that "a
taxpayer has a legislatively imposed responsibility to keep good tax
records." That Court further held that a taxpayer cannot be
permitted "to maintain scant records and after an unsatisfactory tax
audit, avoid taxation by merely verbalizing his transactions
unsupported by appropriate documentation made at the time of the
transactions or by testimony from other parties to the transactions."
In the absence of suitable records, the Taxpayer has the burden of
refuting the Department's estimated assessments. See Weiss v.
Best Enterprises, Inc., 323 Ark. 712, 720, 917 S.W.2d 543, 547
(1996) and Leathers v. A & B Dirt Movers. Inc., 311 Ark. 320, 325,
844 S.W.2d 314, 316-17 (1992); see also Jones v. Ragland, 293 Ark.
320, 323, 737 S.W.2d 641, 643 (1987). The law requires that the
taxpayer offer adequate, credible evidence to establish that the
audit results are unreasonable. Absent adequate supporting
documentation, the Taxpayer lacks sufficient evidence to refute the
reasonableness of the Department's assessments. In Leathers,
supra, the Arkansas Supreme Court discussed the burden of
refuting an assessment, stating:
In short, we find [taxpayer's] testimony insufficient,
standing alone, to meet the taxpayer's statutory burden in
refuting the reasonableness of the assessment. To hold
otherwise would be to permit a taxpayer to maintain scant
records and after an unsatisfactory tax audit, avoid taxation
by merely verbalizing his transactions unsupported by
appropriate documentation made at the time of the
transactions or by testimony from other parties to the
transactions.
Id. at 330, 844 S.W.2d at 319.
D. Penalty and Interest
Interest is required to be assessed upon tax deficiencies for the use
of the State's tax dollars. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-508 (Repl. 2020).
. . . Thus, under the law, interest was required to be assessed in this
case at the time the notice of proposed assessment. Because the
Taxpayer was a non-filer for sales tax, penalty was properly
assessed under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-208 (Repl. 2020). The
Department's assessment of sales and use taxes plus interest was
proper and should be sustained.

The difference between an exclusion and an exemption is
that an exemption pertains to sales that would be covered
were they not specifically exempted from the [Gross
Receipts] Act, while exclusion is simply not included in the
first place. Stated differently, an exemption presupposes a
liability, and is properly applied only to a grant of immunity

The cardinal rule in construing tax legislation is that a tax
cannot be imposed except by express words indicating that purpose,

Based upon the foregoing, , the taxpayer, respectfully
requests that the assessment of Arkansas sales tax, short-term
rental tax, and the assessment of related penalties and interest as
set forth in the Notice of Proposed Assessment be reversed and
dismissed. [Footnotes omitted, P. 1 – 32.]
The Department’s Reply Brief addressed contentions in the Taxpayer’s
Response Brief and stated as follows:
A. Estoppel
The Taxpayer’s first point in its response brief appears to be based
on a theory of estoppel. Specifically, Taxpayer argues that because
the auditor discussed the bundled transaction doctrine in his
emails, and the Department later clarified in its opening brief that
the transactions at issue were not bundled transactions within the
meaning of Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax Rule GR-93, the Office of
Hearings and Appeals may not sustain the tax assessment
regardless of whether the Hearing Officer determines that the
transactions were subject to sales tax. This is incorrect.
First, the Department notes that the Summary of Findings, which
the Department attached to its opening brief as Exhibit 6, states
that the basis for the sales tax adjustments was “Unreported
Taxable Sales.” That is entirely consistent with the arguments and
authorities stated in the Department’s opening brief.
Second, it is unclear whether the hearing officers appointed by the
secretary to hear protests of assessments and refund claim denials
have the authority to render a determination that estoppel should
apply, since this is an equitable power. The provisions of Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-18-405 (Repl. 2020) limit the decisions of the hearing
officer to the application of the relevant law as to the applicability of
32

a proposed assessment or the denial of a claim for refund, and they
do not grant specific authority for decisions based in equity or
fairness. See Bolin v. State, 2015 Ark. 149, at 6, 459 S.W.3d 788,
792 (2015) (holding court may properly construe legislature’s
express designation of one thing to mean the exclusion of another).
Further, even if the statute did provide such specific authority, there
is considerable doubt as to whether the General Assembly has the
constitutional authority to grant equitable powers to an
administrative agency, since the granting of equity is purely a
judicial power. See, e.g., Provenzano v. Long, 64 Nev. 412, 183
P.2d 639 (1947); Mich. Mut. Liability Co. v. Baker, 295 Mich. 237,
294 N.W. 168 (1940), Ford v. Barcus, 261 Iowa 616, 155 N.W.2d
507 (1968) (citing Doyle v. Dugan, 229 Iowa 724, 295 N.W. 128
(1940)).
The Arkansas Supreme Court has held that the defense of estoppel
should not be readily available against the State. See, e.g., Foote’s
Dixie Dandy, Inc. v. McHenry, 270 Ark. 816, 607 S.W.2d 323
(1980). Although it is conceivable that estoppel may arise from a
state employee’s authorized actions, the State of Arkansas, as
sovereign, cannot be bound by its employees unauthorized actions.
See id.; City of Russellville v. Hodges, 330 Ark. 716, 718-19, 957
S.W.2d 690, 691-92 (1997). A court may apply the doctrine of
estoppel against the State only where there is substantial proof and a
compelling reason. Everett v. Jones, 277 Ark. 162, 639 S.W.2d 739
(1982).
A mistake of law – either by the state’s employee or the party
asserting estoppel – will not support an estoppel defense. See
Duchac, 67 Ark. App. at 107-08, 992 S.W.2d at 180 (“It has long
been held that every person is presumed to know the law and that
ignorance of its mandates is no excuse.”); cf. Pambianchi v. Howell,
100 Ark. App. 154, 157, 265 S.W.3d 788, 792 (2007) (holding fraud
cannot be predicated upon misrepresentations as to matters of law,
nor upon opinions on questions of law based on facts known to both
parties alike, nor upon representations as to what the law will not
permit to be done).
Here, in each of the pieces of email correspondence quoted by the
Taxpayer in its response brief, the auditor stated that because the
Taxpayer’s contracts did not separately state the rental of chairs,
tables, and linens – a taxable transaction – from the nontaxable
rental of real property, the Taxpayer owed tax on the entire
transaction. This is entirely consistent with the Department’s
position in its opening brief. The Taxpayer faults the auditor for
citing the bundled transaction doctrine under Arkansas Gross
Receipts Tax Rule GR-93 rather than Weiss v. Best Enterprises,
33

(defining “sale” to include lease or rental of tangible personal
property) and Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-301 (Repl. 2020) (levying 1%
excise tax on short term rental of tangible personal property.
While the Taxpayer asserts that the question of whether the rental
of a venue coupled with the ternal of items of tangible personal
property is a matter of first impression, a review of the Office of
Hearings and Appeals’ hearing decisions, publicly available on the
Department’s website, indicates that the Office of Hearings and
Appeals has considered similar matters in the past. Recently, for
example, in Docket No. 23-001 (Aug. 24, 2022),1 the Office
determined:
The short-term rental of tangible personal property, such as
tables and chairs, is also subject to sales tax and an
additional one percent (1%) excise tax. See Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-52-103(31)(B) (Supp. 2021) (defining “sale” to include
lease or rental of tangible personal property) and Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-63-301 (Repl. 2020) (levying 1% excise tax on
short term rental of tangible personal property). As a
general rule, sales tax applies to the entire gross receipts
from sales of tangible personal property and certain
specifically enumerated services within the State of
Arkansas. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-301 et seq. (Repl.
2020 & Supp. 2021). The liability for collecting and
reporting sales tax is upon the seller of the tangible personal
property or taxable services unless the purchaser claims an
exemption. See Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax Rule GR-
79(A) and (C). Since the [REDACTED] (a lump sum charge)
included the [REDACTED] was subject to tax as a short-
term rental of tangible personal property.
The Hearing Officer sustained the assessment in that case. The facts
of this case mandate a similar result.
C. Sufficient Records
Finally, the Taxpayer, while conceding that its records are not
“exhaustive,” suggests instead that its records are sufficient and
suitable. To be sure, the records that the Taxpayer provided are
sufficient and suitable to establish: (1) the Taxpayer’s rental of
property included the short-term rental of tangible personal
property such as tables, chairs, and linens; (2) the short-term rental
of those items was not separately itemized from the rental of real
property; and (3) the Taxpayer’s documents stated that such items
were “included with every rental” – i.e., not “complimentary.” The
Taxpayer’s post hoc rationalization for failure to collect and remit
35

sales tax is not supported by the contemporaneous documents.
That is why the Supreme Court’s opinion in Leathers v. A & B Dirt
Movers, Inc., 311 Ark. 320, 844 S.W.2d 314 (1992) is applicable
here:
In short, we find [taxpayer’s] testimony insufficient,
standing alone, to meet the taxpayer’s statutory burden in
refuting the reasonableness of the assessment. To hold
otherwise would be to permit a taxpayer to maintain scant
records and after an unsatisfactory tax audit, avoid taxation
by merely verbalizing his transactions unsupported by
appropriate documentation made at the time of the
transactions or by testimony from other parties to the
transactions.
Id. at 330, 844 S.W.2d at 319. Based on the available
documentation, the Taxpayer has failed to meet its statutory burden
of refuting the reasonableness of the sales and use tax assessment.
D. Adjustments consistent with income tax assessment
The Taxpayer, pleading in the alternative, asks the Office and
Hearings and Appeals to require the Department to make certain
adjustments consistent with those the Taxpayers’ subsequent
individual income tax audit. While such a request is outside the
jurisdiction of the Office of Hearings and Appeals, the Department
agrees to make adjustments to the sales tax audit that are consistent
with the subsequent individual income tax audit. [P. 1 – 5.]
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Standard of Proof
Subsection (c) of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313 (Repl. 2020) provides, in
pertinent part, as follows:
The burden of proof applied to matters of fact and evidence,
whether placed on the taxpayer or the state in controversies
regarding the application of a state tax law shall be by
preponderance of the evidence.
In Edmisten v. Bull Shoals Landing, 2014 Ark. 89, at 12-13, 432 S.W.3d 25,
33, the Arkansas Supreme Court explained:
36

A preponderance of the evidence is “not necessarily established by
the greater number of witnesses testifying to a fact but by evidence
that has the most convincing force; superior evidentiary weight
that, though not sufficient to free the mind wholly from all
reasonable doubt, is still sufficient to incline a fair and impartial
mind to one side of the issue rather than the other.”
The Department bears the burden of proving that the tax law applies to an
item or service sought to be taxed, and a taxpayer bears the burden of proving
entitlement to a tax exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(d) (Repl. 2020). Statutes imposing a tax or providing a tax exemption,
deduction, or credit must be reasonably and strictly construed in limitation of
their application, giving the words their plain and ordinary meaning. Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-18-313(a), (b), and (e) (Repl. 2020). If a well-founded doubt exists
with respect to the application of a statute imposing a tax or providing a tax
exemption, deduction, or credit, the doubt must be resolved against the
application of the tax, exemption, deduction, or credit. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
313(f)(2) (Repl. 2020).
Tax Assessments
Subject to the applicability of an exemption, deduction, or a credit, sales
tax is imposed on sales of tangible personal property or taxable services made by
in-state vendors/sellers to in-state purchasers.5 The short-term rental of tangible
personal property, such as tables and chairs,6 is also subject to sales tax and an
additional one percent (1%) excise tax. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-103(31)(B)
(Supp. 2021) (defining “sale” to include lease or rental of tangible personal
property) and Ark. Code Ann. § 26-63-301 (Repl. 2020) (levying 1% excise tax on
5 See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-101 et seq. (Repl. 2020 & Supp. 2021).
6 All references to “tables and chairs” will incorporate all other tangible personal property listed
in the Taxpayer’s contracts.
37

short term rental of tangible personal property). As a general rule, sales tax
applies to the entire gross receipts from sales of tangible personal property and
certain specifically enumerated services within the State of Arkansas. See Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-52-301 et seq. (Repl. 2020 & Supp. 2021). The liability for
collecting and reporting sales tax is upon the seller of the tangible personal
property or taxable services unless the purchaser claims an exemption. See
Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax Rule GR-79(A) and (C).
The rental of venue space, in and of itself, is not an activity that is
specifically subject to tax under Arkansas law. However, since the Taxpayer’s
venue rental fee (a lump sum charge) included the use of tables and chairs, the
venue rental fee was subject to tax as a short-term rental of tangible personal
property (sales tax and an additional one percent (1%) excise tax). As illustrated
in the case of Weiss v. Best Enterprises, Inc., 323 Ark. 712, 917 S.W. 2d 543
(1996), if a taxable item and a nontaxable item are combined on the same invoice,
the entire invoice amount is subject to tax unless the nontaxable item is
separately stated on the invoice.7
The determination in this case is consistent with the Department’s prior
interpretations of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-52-103(31)(B) (Supp. 2021) and Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-63-301 (Repl. 2020). The Arkansas Supreme Court has recognized
that administrative agencies are often required to interpret statutes and rules. In
7 The Department agreed with the Taxpayer that the relevant transactions were “not ‘bundled
transactions’ as defined by the Arkansas law.” See Department’s Opening Brief – P. 4.
Consequently, arguments and issues related to Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax GR-93 are moot and
not addressed in this decision. Any reference or reliance on GR-93 by the Tax Auditor during the
audit did not bar the Department from assessing the Taxpayer for unreported taxable sales.
38

Walnut Grove School Distr. No. 6 of Boone County v. County Board of Education,
204 Ark. 354, 162 S.W.2d 64 (1942), the court’s opinion stated, in part:
. . . the administrative construction generally should be clearly
wrong before it is overturned. Such a construction, commonly
referred to as practical construction, although not controlling, is
nevertheless entitled to considerable weight. It is highly persuasive.
Id. at 359, 162 S.W.2d at 66.
The Taxpayer’s arguments, regarding the distinguishability of this case
from the facts in Weiss v. Best Enterprises, Inc., supra, and that the tables and
chairs were complementary rather than unreported taxable sales, do not establish
that the Department’s prior interpretation was clearly wrong.
The Department has statutory authority to “[a]udit and properly
determine and compute the state tax payable by any taxpayer subject to taxation
under any state law”8 and to “employ proper and reasonable audit methods.”9
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-506 (Repl. 2020) requires the Taxpayer to maintain
suitable records and states:
(a) It is the duty of every taxpayer required to make a return
of any tax due under any state tax law to keep and preserve suitable
records as are necessary to determine the amount of tax due or to
prove the accuracy of any return.
. . .
(d) When a taxpayer fails to preserve and maintain the
records required by any state tax law, the director may, in his or her
discretion, make an estimated assessment based upon
information available to him or her as to the amount of tax due by
the taxpayer. The burden of proof of refuting this estimated
assessment is upon the taxpayer. [Emphasis added].
In the absence of suitable records, the Taxpayer has the burden of refuting
the Department’s estimated assessment. See Jones v. Ragland, 293 Ark. 320, 737
8 See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301(a)(2) (Repl. 2020).
9 See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-305(a)(2)(A) (Repl. 2020).
39

S.W.2d 641 (1987); Leathers v. A. & B. Dirt Movers, Inc., 311 Ark. 320, 844
S.W.2d 314 (1992); Weiss v. Best Enterprises, Inc., 323 Ark. 712, 917 S.W.2d 543
(1996). The law requires that sufficient credible evidence be offered by the
Taxpayer to establish that the audit results are unreasonable.
The Taxpayer failed to maintain sufficient records to determine the
amount of tax due (tables and chairs not separately stated from rental of real
property on invoices or contracts). The Department used the best information
available (bank records) to calculate the assessment. The Taxpayer did not
maintain sales invoices, or all of its contracts, so use of the income reflected on
the bank records was necessary and reasonable. The Taxpayer failed to establish
that the audit methodology or calculations used by the Department were
unreasonable. Since the Taxpayer was not reporting any taxable sales during the
audit period, the Taxpayer was underreporting by more than twenty-five percent
(25%) and a six-year audit period was authorized under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-
306(e) (Repl. 2020).
The Taxpayer failed to present sufficient documentation to meet the
burden of refuting the estimated assessment of tax. See Jones v. Ragland, supra
and Leathers v. A. & B. Dirt Movers, Inc., supra. Consequently, the evidence
presented supports a finding that the Department correctly assessed tax against
the Taxpayer.
Interest
With respect to the assessment of interest protested by the Taxpayer, Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-18-508 (Repl. 2020) states, in part:
40

Interest shall be collected on tax deficiencies and paid on
overpayments as follows:
. . .
(2) Interest on a tax deficiency shall be assessed at the same
time as the tax deficiency. The tax deficiency together with the
interest shall be paid upon notice and demand by the Secretary of
the Department of Finance and Administration; [Emphasis added].
It is noteworthy that the statute establishing the assessment and collection
of interest on a tax deficiency utilizes the term “shall.” Utilization of the term
“shall” indicates a mandatory action. Based on the mandatory statutory
language, the Office of Hearings and Appeals does not have the discretion to
waive the assessment of interest. Interest was properly assessed upon the tax
deficiency for the use of the State’s tax dollars. See Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-508
(Repl. 2020).
Penalty
The only assertion made by the Department regarding the assessed
penalty was that, “[b]ecause the Taxpayer was a non-filer for sales tax, penalty
was properly assessed under Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-208 (Repl. 2020).”10
Arkansas Gross Receipts Tax Rule GR-85(C) addresses the failure to file penalty
and states that, “[n]o penalty will be assessed if the failure to file is due to
reasonable cause and not to willful neglect.”
The Taxpayer asserted that reasonable cause was demonstrated in this
case because this assessment arose from the Taxpayer’s first audit and the
Taxpayer had relied on professional tax advice. The Department’s Reply Brief
asserted that a previously considered case involving “similar matters” was
10 See Department’s Opening Brief – P. 7.
41

sustained by this Office and the facts of this case mandate a “similar result.”
Significantly, it should be noted that no penalty was assessed against the taxpayer
in the prior case involving “similar matters.”
The arguments of the parties and the evidence presented in this matter
preponderate in favor of a finding that the Taxpayer’s failure to file was due to
reasonable cause rather than willful neglect. The assessments of penalty are not
sustained.
DECISION AND ORDER
Subject to the agreed upon adjustments, the proposed assessments are
sustained, in part.11 The tax and interest portions of the sales and special excise
tax assessments are sustained. The penalty portions of the sales and special
excise tax assessments are set aside.
The file is to be returned to the appropriate section of the Department for
further proceedings in accordance with this Administrative Decision and
applicable law. Pursuant to Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-405 (Repl. 2020), unless the
Taxpayer requests in writing within twenty (20) days of the mailing of this
decision that the Commissioner of Revenues revise the decision of the
Administrative Law Judge, this Administrative Decision shall be effective and
become the action of the agency. The revision request may be mailed to the
Assistant Commissioner of Revenues, P.O. Box 1272, Rm. 2440, Little Rock,
Arkansas 72203.
11 The use tax assessment was not contested. Other than the adjustments agreed upon by the
Department, there is insufficient documentation in the case file to support a finding that
additional adjustments to taxable sales (discussed in Section 5 of the Taxpayer’s Response Brief)
are warranted.
42

A revision request may also be faxed to the Assistant Commissioner of
Revenues at (501) 683-1161 or emailed to revision@dfa.arkansas.gov. The
Commissioner of Revenues, within twenty (20) days of the mailing of this
Administrative Decision, may revise the decision regardless of whether the
Taxpayer has requested a revision.
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-406 (Repl. 2020) provides for the judicial appeal
of a final decision of an Administrative Law Judge or the Commissioner of
Revenues on a final assessment or refund claim denial; however, the
constitutionality of that code section is uncertain.12

FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Standard of Proof
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(c) (Supp. 2019) provides, in pertinent part, as
follows:
